entry.title: The Very Best Earplugs for Sleeping
entry.summary: From disposable foam to reusable silicone to earbuds that play white noise.
entry.content:
When choosing the right earplugs for sleep, there are two main considerations: comfort and effectiveness. If the earplugs feel irritating or too noticeable — especially on a sensitive area like your ears — you probably still won’t be able to sleep well. And if they don’t actually block out noise, then what’s the point?

To find the best earplugs for sleeping, I spoke to sleep experts and earplug users about their favorite earplugs to sleep in, as well as what to consider when shopping. I also tested several pairs myself to judge how effective and comfortable they are. Below, you’ll find a mix of disposable and reusable earplugs, made from a range of materials. Or, if you’d rather mask noise than block it out entirely, take a look at our guide to the best sound machines.

Update on November 4, 2026
I named the Crystal Guardian Sleep Plugs the best custom earplugs for sleep. I also added notes on two pairs I tried and didn’t love and verified pricing and availability for all the earplugs we recommend.

What an earplug is made of will dictate how it feels and fits in your ear. Several experts mentioned soft foam or silicone as the best options for comfort. These materials seem to be the most common, though there are others, including wax, as well as more advanced earbud designs that play audio. Neurologist Dr. Chris Winter says foam earplugs are the best to “muffle out the higher pitched sounds and quiet the whole environment down.” Dr. Raj Dasgupta generally agrees, recommending soft foam earplugs because they’ll gently expand in the ear to fit comfortably in the ear canal and effectively block out noise. However, Dasgupta says some people might find silicone more comfortable if they have sensitive ears.

Earplugs should always come with a noise-reduction rating (NRR) or single-noise rating (SNR), which measures how effectively they reduce noise. In the United States, earplugs are typically rated with the NRR. The higher the NRR, the more effective the earplug. The highest NRR for earplugs is 33, so that’s what to look for if you are seeking maximum silence while you sleep. However, a 33 NRR may not be totally necessary for sleep — the measurement is primarily used to gauge ear protection from potentially damaging sounds, such as those from loud machinery or music. While you may need to block out sound to be able to sleep, odds are your ears aren’t in danger from high noise levels at night.

Most earplugs have an NRR between 20 and 30, and a rating in that range should keep nighttime noise at bay. I’ve included each earplug’s NRR below, but keep in mind that other factors, like how well the earplugs fit your ears, can change how effective they are. If you buy earplugs from another country (particularly ones in the European Union or the United Kingdom), you may see they are rated with the SNR rather than (or in addition to) the NRR. The general principle is the same: A higher rating equals more noise reduction and ear protection.

In general, foam and wax earplugs tend to be disposable, while silicone or plastic ones tend to be infinitely reusable, or at least reusable for a quite a long time. Disposable earplugs are typically meant to be used just once, or for a few nights at maximum. 

Reusable earplugs will have a higher upfront cost for one pair, but depending on how often you are using earplugs, they may be a lot more cost-effective over time. For all the earplugs below, I’ve listed the cost per pair and for the disposable ones, I’ve also included the total price per package. 

Overall, I prefer reusable earplugs so that I don’t need to regularly repurchase them, plus they don’t create as much waste as disposable ones. However, if you prefer the feel of soft foam or wax earplugs, or if you’re looking for a cheap option that you also don’t have to clean or keep track of, disposable might be a better choice for you. Though most reusable earplugs come with a carrying case, they are ultimately still small and easy to lose.

Material: Thermoplastic | Type: Reusable | Noise-reduction rating: 16 | Single-noise rating: 22 | Price: $25 for one pair

The Alpine Silence earplugs check all the boxes I want for a reusable sleep earplug: They are unobtrusive, comfortable, reasonably priced, and effective at blocking noise. They are made from Alpine’s proprietary thermoplastic material, which is silicone-free but feels extremely similar to silicone. (They’re also latex-free and hypoallergenic.) The earplugs are quite pliant — I can easily bend them with my fingers, and the thermoplastic becomes more moldable when warm — but they always retain their shape.

What makes these earplugs stand out is the V-shaped external piece, which fits snugly into the concha of my ear (the flat part next to the opening of the ear canal). The overall design of the Alpines is similar to many other earplugs on the market (see the Loop and Curvd earplugs discussed below), but that V-shape makes the outer part of the earplug quite small and allows it to lay flatter in my ear than other styles I’ve tried. This also makes the Alpine Silence earplugs an especially great pick for side sleepers.

The other design detail I really appreciate about the Alpines is the oval shape of the ear tip (the part that actually goes into your ear canal), which allows for a more snug fit in the ear, and ultimately blocks sound better, than rounder designs. The Alpine Silence earplugs come with four sizes of ear tips — extra small, small, medium, and large — so you can try different sizes to find the one that fits best. My pair came preloaded with the medium ear tips, but I ended up swapping them for the small ones.

I also think the Alpine Silence earplugs are a good deal. One $25 pair could easily last years; the earplugs can be washed with soap and water to keep them clean, and other than losing or damaging them, there’s no real reason to replace them. Alpine provides a small carrying case to store them in, too.

Material: Silicone | Type: Reusable | Single-noise rating: 25 | Price: 3 pairs for $22.95 ($7.65 per pair)

When I went on a hunt to find the best earplugs for concerts, Earpeace’s Music earplugs earned the top spot for their good protection, comfortable fit, and affordable price. I was excited to learn that the brand’s Sleep earplugs checked many of the same boxes as the Music version. The Earpeace Sleep earplugs have a similar tiered, conical design with a pull-tab for easy insertion and removal. They’re made from flexible silicone and feature a silicone sound filter, which Earpeace says reduces noise by up to 30dB. Instead of totally blocking sound, these are designed to dim it to a “comfortable level for restful sleep.” Even with that caveat, the earplugs did a good job of blocking out noise in my apartment, especially since the tiered design provides a secure fit. They fit comfortably in my ears, even while side sleeping, and didn’t put pressure on my ears.

Earpeace offers two size options, standard and small; the former is designed to fit about 80 percent of people. I tend to need smaller earplugs, so I tried the small size and they fit my ears well. Earpeace provides you with three pairs of earplugs for the same price that most brands charge for just one, but they don’t give you the option to order both sizes together to find the right fit, as some other brands do. They also don’t have any customization options, such as changeable ear tips, like the Alpine earplugs above. Still, you get three pairs of Earpeace Sleep earplugs for the price of one pair from Alpine, making the Earpeace an affordable choice for comfortable and effective reusable earplugs.

Material: Thermoplastic | Type: Reusable up to 100 times | Noise-reduction rating: 27 | Price: Starting at as $17 for one pair (or $19 for two pairs, one in each size)

If you want a reusable earplug that’s soft like a disposable foam earplug, I recommend the Alpine SleepDeep earplugs. Like my top-pick Alpine Silence earplugs, they are made from the brand’s proprietary thermoplastic material, which absorbs your body heat to mold to fit your ear. However, it feels very different on the SleepDeep earplugs; where the Alpine Silence earplugs have a similar texture to a silicone spatula, the thermoplastic on the SleepDeep earplugs is much thinner and more flexible — more like a deflated balloon. Thanks to the soft, moldable material and cone-like shape, the SleepDeep earplugs fit very snugly into my ear, without much material sticking out (there is a small pull flap for easy removal).

The Alpine SleepDeep earplugs are just as soft as the disposable Mack’s earplugs below, but they are designed to be reused up to 100 times. In my testing, they didn’t block quite as much noise as the Mack’s — the Mack’s have a higher NRR of 33, compared to the SleepDeep’s 27 — but they are still very effective (and still have a higher NRR than my top pick for a reusable earplug, the Alpine Silence).

The SleepDeep earplugs come in three sizes, small, medium, and large. If you know which size you want, you can order one pair for $16. If you want to try both, a set with one pair in each size only costs $3 more. I tried the multipack and ended up preferring the size small. They also come with a small carrying case.

Material: Foam | Type: Disposable | Noise-reduction rating: 33 | Price: 50 pairs for $15 ($.30 per pair)

If there’s one brand name I heard more than any other while reporting this guide, it was Mack’s. The effective noise-blocking, comfortable feel, and cheap price of these earplugs make them my top pick for disposable earplugs for sleep.

They’ve been recommended by multiple people, including someone who lives on a busy Brooklyn street with lots of traffic noise and another who has hyperacusis, a condition that causes extreme sound sensitivity. Based on those recommendations, I tried the Mack’s earplugs myself. I’ve used these types of foam earplugs many times in the past, especially for concerts. However, the foam used for Mack’s is considerably softer than the foam on earplugs designed more for hearing protection. This soft foam definitely makes for a more comfortable fit while sleeping.

I was also extremely impressed with how much noise these earplugs can block; they are easily some of the most effective earplugs I’ve tried to date. My experience tracks with that of writer Lisa McCarty, the Mack’s user with hyperacusis, who says, “They reduce the sounds of everything from construction noise to background conversation, making the room go quiet. It’s almost a meditative state when I put them in, as it helps me focus on my breathing instead of the noise and stimulation outside.”

Mack’s earplugs have the highest possible NRR at 33, but they also plug the ear canal more than the other styles I’ve tried, which can take some getting used to. To put them in, you pinch the foam, insert the earplug, then let it expand in your ear, which creates a very thorough seal. One drawback is that if you twist the foam too tight, the earplugs may push uncomfortably on your ear once expanded, so you may need to practice a few times. Between their comfort, effective noise blocking, and affordable price, Mack’s definitely earns the top spot for disposable earplugs.

Material: Foam | Type: Disposable | Noise-reduction rating: 31 | Price: 50 pairs for $15 ($.30 per pair)

If you struggle to find earplugs that fit your smaller ears, these Slim Fit disposable earplugs from Mack’s come highly recommended by Jeff Kahn, the founder and CEO of the RISE app. Kahn has been using these earplugs for over 10 years and says they are comfortable for sleeping — even on his side — and that the “slow release, low-pressure, and tapered foam means they get a good seal and don’t exert that familiar pressure feel from inside the ear.” Overall, these are pretty similar to our top pick, just with a slimmer profile for small ears. They do have a slightly lower NRR than the other Mack’s, but 31 is still a very high NRR.

Material: Mycelium | Type: Disposable | Noise-reduction rating: 20 | Price: 12 pairs for $24.95 ($2.08 per pair)

Aside from the inconvenience of having to resupply, the biggest drawback to disposable earplugs is the waste they produce. Most disposable earplugs are made from some form of single-use plastic, typically polyurethane foam. GOB’s earplugs are instead made from farm-grown mycelium, the underground root network of fungi, so they are completely biodegradable. They’re also hypoallergenic and, technically, they are even edible — which, while not advised, may be of some reassurance if someone inadvertently swallows one.

GOB earplugs look similar to a disposable foam earplug, though they are more cylindrical than cone shaped. They’re soft and feel even lighter than traditional foam earplugs. Because of the off-white color, they look more “natural” than typical foam, but I wouldn’t be able to tell they are made of mycelium just by looking at them (and, no, they don’t smell like mushrooms).

When I tested the GOB earplugs, I initially tried to insert one the same way I would a foam earplug: by squeezing the end and letting it expand in my ear for a proper seal. However, that ended up squishing the earplug so that it was unusable, so I consulted the directions (as I should have done to begin with) and learned that the proper way to insert them is even simpler: Place them in your ear and gently press the outer end in until secure. I tried that with a new pair, and the earplugs nestled into my ear comfortably. I wasn’t able to get the same thorough seal I associate with foam earplugs, but the GOB earplugs were actually more comfortable than traditional foam — perhaps because the mycelium is so lightweight, they felt less obtrusive in my ear. When I slept in them, they didn’t block quite as much noise as others I’ve tried, but they were easily able to erase the sounds of my downstairs neighbors. I was worried the earplugs wouldn’t stay secure, but I didn’t have any issue with them coming out.

The main drawback for the GOB earplugs is definitely the price — at almost $2 per pair, they aren’t cheap. If you decide you like them, you can save a little more by springing for the 30-count Sustain Pack for $55, or setting up a recurring subscription to get 15 percent off. But for the earplug wearer who wants a sustainable, disposable option, GOB earplugs are pretty great.

[Editor’s note: The GOB earplugs are currently unavailable. We’ve reached out to the company for further information about when they’ll be restocked.]

Material: Silicone | Type: Reusable | Noise-reduction rating: 14 | Single-noise rating: 24 | Price: $25 for one pair

I was a longtime user of Loop’s Experience 2 earplugs to protect my ears at concerts, and several fellow Strategist staffers have told me they use different models of Loop earplugs for a variety of reasons, so I was eager to try the Loop Quiet earplugs, which block more noise than the Experience model. The earplugs’ design is pretty similar to audio earbuds — they have a silicone ear tip that goes into the opening of the ear canal and a loop-shaped external piece that you can hold as you put them in and take them off. Like my top-pick Alpine Silence earplugs, they come with four sizes of ear tips — extra small, small, medium, and large — to ensure a good fit. Mine arrived with the medium tips already on, which ended up being the best size for my ears. They also come with a small carrying case.

The Loop earplugs have a slightly lower NRR of 14 compared to the Alpines’ NRR of 16, but they easily blocked the sound of a TV in the next room while I took a nap. They sit snugly, without feeling pressurized or tight, and the small loop rests by the flat part of my ear. They are plenty comfortable for sleeping, and I didn’t feel any pressure while lying on my side. Overall, the Loop Quiet earplugs are very similar to the Alpine ones above, with slight differences in shape — the Loop Quiet ear-tips are a bit rounder, and the external piece is a circular “loop” instead of a V. Ultimately, I found the Alpine’s V-shaped external piece and more oval ear tips a touch more comfortable, which is why the edged out the Loop Quiets for the top spot in this guide. But if you think the Loop Quiet’s shape will better fit your ears, or you have a preference for silicone over the Alpines’ thermoplastic, the Loop Quiet is also a really great earplug.

Material: Silicone | Type: Reusable for a limited time | Noise-reduction rating: 22 | Price: 8 pairs for $17 ($2.13 per pair)

If you’d rather not stick an earplug into your ear canal, these moldable silicone earplugs act more like a cap to the ear canal. To use them, you warm up the silicone by rolling it around in your hands, then press and flatten into the center of the external part of your ear. At first, this process felt a little like sticking Play-Doh into my ears (in line with the name Squishies). But once I got the silicone molded and flattened, I was really impressed with both how comfortable the earplugs felt and how much noise they blocked. The pieces of silicone are pretty large, but you can break them into smaller pieces if needed.

These earplugs come in a pack of eight and are reusable, according to the Eargasm customer service representative I spoke to. But they will eventually have to be replaced after extended use. However, I think you should be able to get decent mileage out of them, which might justify the slightly higher cost per pair, compared to some of the other earplugs on this list (minus the infinitely reusable ones).

Material: Wax | Type: Disposable | Noise-reduction rating: 23 | Price: $7 for 6 pairs ($1.17 per pair)

These wax earplugs come recommended by two sources we spoke to, both of whom like them for their moldability. They are very similar to the Eargasm Squishies, above, and fit into the outer ear, not directly into the ear canal. “They do an outstanding job of conforming to the ear to block out sound,” says Bill Fish, former president of Sleep Doctor. “But they are also quite comfortable, as they come with a soft cotton cover around the wax.” If you want a moldable earplug that is not made of silicone, these are a good choice. However, because they are disposable, they will cost a bit more in the long run.

Material: Silicone | Type: Reusable | Noise-reduction rating: No rating; Crystal Guardian says they reduce sound by 28 to 30dBs | Price: $110 base price for custom plugs; $25 extra for glitter; $5 extra for a carrying case

For the best fit, you can’t beat custom earplugs. Popular among frequent concertgoers, Crystal Guardian’s custom designs are especially fun thanks to the vast catalogue of color (and glitter) options to choose from. Senior writer Michael Zhao purchased a pair a few months ago and says they are “crazy good” — in fact, they block sound so well he’s had to pause using them at night to make sure he hears his newborn baby when she cries. Zhao says the silicone is soft in his ear and the fact that they are custom-shaped eliminates any discomfort or pressure. “It’s basically like not having ear canals,” he says.

The Sleep Plugs are made entirely from silicone without the filters Crystal Guardian puts in its musician earplugs. They also have a pull tab that follows the shape of the ear, so you can easily remove them without any pieces sticking out and making it uncomfortable to sleep on your side. Because they are custom molded, you’ll have to get ear impressions done before you can purchase a pair. Zhao did this at Crystal Guardian in Brooklyn, but you can go to any audiologist and have them send the impressions to the company. Of course, between the effort (and potential cost) of getting the impressions done and the over-$100 price tag for the earplugs, these are a much bigger commitment than my other reusable picks. But if you haven’t found a pair of mass-produced earplugs that fit your ears comfortably or effectively block enough sound, Crystal Guardian’s may be worth a try. “If you live next to a bar, these are a must-buy. The difference between these and foam earplugs is like comparing a car to a bicycle,” says Zhao.

Material: Earbuds with silicone ear tips | Type: Reusable | Noise-reduction rating: N/A | Price: $200 for one pair

I was really interested in these Bluetooth sleep earbuds because I love listening to a podcast when I’m taking a nap or even just lying down to rest — it calms my mind and helps prevent me from overthinking. But many earbuds are at least a little uncomfortable to sleep in because of how they stick out of your ear. Because the Soundcore earbuds are specifically designed for sleep, they are impressively unobtrusive, with a flatter external design and a silicone wing tip that acts like a cushion between the harder pieces of the earbud and your ear. They come with three different wing-tip sizes to try, as well as four sizes of sealed ear tips for noise blocking and three sizes of “breathable” ear tips that allow for more airflow but don’t block noise. This level of customization makes the earbuds especially versatile.

I first tested the Soundcore A20 earbuds a couple of years ago and was impressed by how comfortable they were, as well as the decent sound quality they offered. However, I’ve more recently been testing the newer A30 model, and I think the A30s are a solid improvement on the original. The A30 earbuds have a slightly more oblong shape than the A20s, which are perfectly round. It’s a slight difference, but I found the shape change made them even better suited to resting in my ear. The silicone ear tips also feel softer and more flexible. And while I’m no audiophile, I think the sound quality is improved as well — not quite as good as that of my AirPods, but closer. The A30 earbuds also have a host of new features the A20 earbuds don’t offer, like active noise cancellation and snore masking. I haven’t gotten a great sense of how well the snore-masking feature works, as my husband doesn’t really snore, but they cancel noise fairly well. When I wear them for a nap, I’m rarely distracted by sounds around me.

The accompanying app has plenty of features worth exploring, including white noise, nature/ASMR-esque sounds, and meditations and sleep stories from the popular Calm app. Of course, you can also play your own audio by switching from “local” listening to the Bluetooth mode. It’s an easy toggle, though it is an extra step compared to popping in my AirPods to listen to a podcast. In the app, you can also set auto-off timers, bedtime reminders, and in-ear alarms and get a report on how well you slept. I don’t use these features as much, but I could see them being handy. The battery life is also quite impressive. I don’t wear these earbuds to sleep every night — I mostly use them for taking naps — but I’ve only had to charge them once over the past few months. For daily use, Soundcore says they’ll stay charged for eight to ten hours.

The A30 earbuds are slightly more expensive than their predecessors, so if you want to save a little money, the A20 earbuds I’ve listed below are still a good option. However, I think the upgrades to the A30s, like the improved comfort and noise reduction, make the additional cost worthwhile. And the A30s are still cheaper than competing products such as the Ozlo Sleepbuds or NextSense Smartbuds.

I previously named Curvd’s reusable silicone Everyday earplugs the Best (Less Expensive) Silicone earplugs because they are very similar to the Loop Quiet earplugs, for about $5 less. While I still think the Curvd earplugs are a perfectly acceptable choice, their outer piece is noticeably larger than that of both the Loop Quiet earplugs and my top-pick Alpine Silence earplugs. The silicone of the Curvd earplugs also doesn’t feel as soft, flexible, or comfortable as Loop’s silicone or Alpine’s thermoplastic. Given the minimal price difference, especially over time, I recommend paying the extra five bucks for either the Alpines or the Loops.

These minimal, Swedish-designed thermoplastic earplugs come in three sizes, but instead of changing the ear tips, as with many of our reusable picks above, you can buy each size individually or get a Discovery Pack with all three. They also come in an array of seasonal and limited-edition colors, as well as recycled-plastic and ocean-plastic versions. Strategist lead editor Lauren Levy previously tested these on a quest to find earplugs for small ears, but I retested them to get firsthand experience. I got the Discovery Pack, which came with three sizes of earplugs and a small case for each pair. The small pair fit my ears well and were very effective at blocking noise, but they just weren’t comfortable for side sleeping. The earplugs felt fine while lying on my back, but when I turned onto my side, I could feel pressure on my ear due to the long external piece that protrudes from the ear. If you are a dedicated back sleeper, these may work well. Otherwise, I think they are better suited for non-sleep uses.

I tried Hears’ high-fidelity earplugs when hunting for the best concert earplugs, and while they didn’t end up being my favorite, I was curious to give the sleep version a try when they launched in 2026. Ultimately, like the Hears concert earplugs, these were just fine. They blocked out sound perfectly well, and I appreciate that they come with a carrying case and four ear-tip sizes. But I didn’t find the fit quite as comfortable as that of my other favorite reusable pairs. The ear tips are more circular than the Alpine Silence’s oval-shaped ones, which makes these feel bulkier in my ear. Overall, I think there are better and more affordable options.

These Bollsen earplugs have a similar design to some earplugs I recommend, such as the Earpeace Sleep or Alpine SleepDeep: a conical shape with multiple rings. They are made of silicone and fairly soft and pliant, which I like. And in testing, I found they blocked noise effectively (the Life+ earplugs have an SNR of 24 and NRR of 17). But I didn’t think they fit as comfortably in my ear as the other conical earplugs I’ve tried. The earplugs are noticeably larger than the Earpeace or Alpine offerings, and because I have small ears, the bigger size created some uncomfortable pressure. I didn’t try this, but Bollsen offers a service that uses AI to match your ear size from photos you take at home, which costs an additional $24. However, when you purchase a standard pair online, there is only one size option. If you have larger ears, they may work well for you.

Toward the end of 2024, Loop released a new sleep earplug called the Loop Dream, which I tested to compare to the Quiet earplugs above. The Dream earplugs have the same basic design as the Quiet earplugs, but the external “loop” is covered in another layer of silicone that makes it feel a little softer and more pliant. (The extra silicone didn’t make a huge difference, comfort-wise, for me, but if the Loop Quiet feels too stiff, the Dreams may be more comfortable.) Another design difference is that the Dream ear tips are made from foam covered with silicone and have a more pointed, oval-like shape than the rounder Loop Quiets (which also makes them more similar to my top pick Alpines). This design creates a more sealed “plug” in your ear but also meant I had to push the earplugs further into my ears to get them to stay in place. Like the Quiet earplugs, the Dream earplugs come with four sizes of ear tips. Even though I liked the medium ear tips for the Quiet, I ended up sizing all the way down to extra small for the Dream earplugs.

The Dream earplugs have a higher NNR than the Quiet earplugs (21 versus 14), so they are rated to block out more noise. I did notice a slight difference in noise reduction, but it wasn’t major. All in all, I think the Dream earplugs are probably a slightly better earplug for sleeping than the Quiet, but they also cost twice as much, and I didn’t think they were better enough to justify the price jump. With that in mind, I’d still pick the Loop earplugs as my top choice for a reusable silicone earplug. But if you don’t like the Loop Quiet, want a higher noise rating, or don’t care about spending double, the Loop Dream earplugs are a solid choice.

• Dr. Michael Breus, clinical psychologist and fellow of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
• Dr. Raj Dasgupta, pulmonary, critical care, and sleep specialist
• Bill Fish, former president at Sleep Doctor
• Jeff Kahn, founder and CEO of RISE app
• Lisa McCarty, writer and women’s health advocate
• Dr. Chris Winter, neurologist and author of The Sleep Solution

Additional reporting by Lauren Levy, Louis Cheslaw, and Karen Iorio Adelson.

entry.title: New Stuff Alert: Dimepiece-Designed Timex and a Giant Manchego Cheese Wheel
entry.summary: Plus, two new cool-guy shoe collabs.
entry.content:
For this week’s “Don’t Dillydally,” we’ve rounded up a range of newly released products we’re particularly excited about, including a Sperry and Colbo collaboration, Alex Mill’s winter collection, and Play-Doh for adults.

Two of watch world’s coolest tastemakers — Dimepiece founder Brynn Wallner and Foundwell’s Alan Bedwell — have released their second collaboration with Timex. This “Blackout” edition of the Intrepid decks it out in an all-black stainless steel case and strap. And at just $269, it’s a relatively affordable gift option for the watch guy (or girl) in your life.

Channel your inner Gwynnie with Caddis’s new frame silhouette, designed in collaboration with Goop. The aviator-shaped GWYN comes in three colorways — gold with green lenses, gunmetal with blue lenses, and gold with clear brown — and is available in both readers and progressive lenses.

Six pounds of Spain’s finest Manchego, sourced by Flamingo Estate from cheesemaker Quesería 1605, located in La Mancha. With notes of toasted pineapple, almond, and marzipan, this makes a super special gift (or keep it on hand to carve away during all of your upcoming holiday hosting).

Is there any brand Sperry hasn’t collaborated with? But we must admit this is a particularly good one with Colbo, which has designed a very interesting loafer that the brand describes as “somewhere between a vintage suiting shoe and a ballet flat.” The low vamp also offers plenty of opportunities to show off some colorful socks.

Speaking of footwear collabs, cool-guy shop NN.07 has teamed up with Clarks to jazz up their Desert Boot and their Wallabees. Launching on November 9, the Desert Boot in particular caught our eye with its jaunty buckle — Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao described them as “very Renn Fayre,” in a good way.

Two Gen Z-favored brands, Heaven Mayhem and Ouai, have made two wearable perfume pendants. One is designed in a two-tone metallic finish and stores Ouai’s floral Rue St. Honoré scent; the other is black and silver with a very on-trend black tassel and houses the warmer Ibiza scent. Bookmark now for your college-age niece whom you never know what to buy for the holidays.

Two of our favorite brands — Fujifilm and Cotopaxi — have this fun kit out which includes a Fujifilm Instax Mini 13 camera, a Cotopaxi Camera Shoulder Bag, a Cotopaxi Camera Strap, and a Cotopaxi Accessory Bag, plus plenty of film.

Alex Mill’s new winter collection is supremely cozy with plenty of fair isle sweaters and faux fur to keep you warm until April. Strategist senior editor Hilary Reid is particularly fond of the candy-stripe cardigan, and I’ve personally got my eye on a pair of the velvet flats.

Even Play-Doh is getting in on the romantasy game and has released a floral craft kit inspired by Sarah J. Maas’s A Court of Thorns and Roses series. While AO3 is down, it might be nice to have something to do with your hands.

entry.title: The Strategist Guide to Shopping at Free People
entry.summary: It’s not all prairie dresses.
entry.content:
Anyone who has shopped at a retailer with few physical storefronts knows it can be hard to figure out where to begin. There are lots of options that all seem as worthy as the next, but the reality is that products from any given brand are not all created equal. When you shop as regularly as we do, you learn that many brands just do some things better than they do other things. With a vast collection of flowy silhouettes and vintage-inspired staples, Free People is one of those brands.

When it comes to browsing at the boho retailer (owned by the same parent company as Urban Outfitters and Anthropologie), the main challenges are that many styles from We the Free, its in-house label, are quick to sell out, and some are only available for a single season. To help you find the best (in stock) clothing, activewear, accessories, and more, we’ve rounded up every Free People item from our archive — including our favorite bikini-cut underwear for women, our best henley cashmere sweater, and the adjustable sling bag one writer owns multiples of.

Updated on November 4, 2026
I added an all-cotton white tee, cashmere henley, and more items we’ve recommended this year to this list. I also made sure all items below are in stock and priced correctly.

When we asked cool teens about their favorite jeans, this loose, barrel-y pair from Free People was name-dropped by one 18-year-old college student in New York. She likes their exaggerated shape, but says they’re less pronounced than some other barrel jeans.

This summer, our writer Tembe Denton-Hurst interviewed other stylish women who wear anywhere from a size 12 to a 20 about where they’re getting their clothes. Free People’s flowy and oversize pieces were highlighted for being surprisingly roomy, even if the sizing only goes up to 16 or XL. “I’ve been wearing Free People since high school. I have five pairs of those barrel jeans,” says beauty and fashion editor Aniyah Morinia.

When I went searching for a new boxy white tee to replace a (now discontinued) Organic Basics T-shirt, I decided to test out the 100 percent cotton CC Tee from Free People. Though it didn’t go on to become the ultimate winner, I appreciated the lightweight slub texture and slouchy construction as well as the raw edges and folded detailing on the sleeves. It was perfect for layering over a bathing suit in the summer and I’ve paired it with high-waisted jeans this fall.

Our writer Kitty Guo was immediately drawn to this sweater when visiting a Free People store, and it was recently named our best henley cashmere sweater overall. Guo loved the supersoft cashmere and versatile weight: “I feel like a lot of cashmere sweaters seem as though they’re meant to keep you feeling very warm and bundled up for cold weather, but this one is sort of more relaxed and feels like you can wear it through fall and spring too,” Guo says.

While on the hunt for the perfect culottes, our senior fashion writer Ambar Pardilla couldn’t decide between Free People’s Ivy and Lucca. “They’re the culotte-iest of the culottes I tried,” Pardilla says. “I wanted all the comforts of a pant, shorts, and skirt in a culotte, and I got all the comforts of a pant, shorts, and skirt in these culottes.” She called out the just-right length and that each pair is made from 100 percent cotton. “They have a fullness that’s very laissez-faire,” Pardilla added.

Here’s another beachy piece I’m hoping to wear on vacation. Made from a blend of breezy linen and cotton, this pull-on skort looks ideal for throwing on as a cover-up. Just note: It has a micro silhouette (just as the product name describes) so it’s extra short, but since it’s a skort, it has built-in shorts for added coverage.

Free People really shines on the summer-dress front. Contributor Talia Mayden tried two of the brand’s dresses while on her hunt for the perfect no-bra summer-heat-wave dress — the Full of Sunshine minidress, and the Me and You midi slip — and while neither was exactly perfect, she liked both. The minidress “floated right over my head and over my hips flawlessly” and was a steal at $60. And the silk midi looks and fits like a high-end vintage option might, and it doesn’t require dry cleaning.

When we polled experts about the best workout leggings, Vanessa Chu, the co-founder of Stretch’d, recommended these seamless leggings for yoga or Pilates. Chu, who is a certified yoga instructor, says the spandex and nylon material is not too thick or thin, which means these offer temperature regulation and proper coverage. A perforated panel on the back of the legs provides added breathability, while the UV-protective fabric shields against sun exposure. They’re also available in 15 colors, from lime green to basic black.

On her search for baggy workout pants to wear comfortably in a post-leggings world, Druckman tested a dozen picks from popular activewear brands. She described this FP Movement style as being a slouchy pair you can wear from Pilates to brunch since they’re lightweight and flowy. “They hit right at my ankle, and the cinched bottom hems prevent the pants from riding up my leg throughout the workout,” she says.

This design also caught Druckman’s attention: At the thigh, they resemble leggings, but the bubble shape around the ankles gives them a baggier illusion that would be ideal for yoga classes.

A few seasons ago, former Strategist editor Maxine Builder purchased this onesie, which is inspired by the Good Karma leggings above, according to the product description. Builder says the fabric is fairly thin and surprisingly soft — but pretty supportive, given the crisscross, open-back silhouette. The jumpsuit also has a perforated design around the hips and down the legs, which means it’s better for summer or sweaty activities like hot yoga, Builder says. She owns this Washed Black colorway and says it doesn’t show sweat.

Another supportive one-piece is the Righteous Runsie, which I tested for this story. It combines a comfortable tank-style top with lightweight (and lined) shorts. It’s great for low-to-medium-impact workouts, such as Pilates and strength training, though I also wear it while doing quick errands. It also has a center cutout and a zippered back pocket, ideal for stashing my cards or lip balm. I own it in black, though it’s available in over a dozen other colors, including light pink, brown, and navy blue.

I was also sent these running shorts, and they have quickly become my go-to for humid runs. They are exceptionally lightweight, and the mesh zippered waistband is almost like a running belt with plenty of space to stash small items such as my house keys or energy gels. I own them in this hot-pink shade, but I’m already eyeing more colors for the fall.

This pullover appeared in our fleece-jacket guide, as recommended by style blogger Bethany Everett-Ratcliffe. “It’s most comparable to the brand’s older Nantucket Fleece, which I have and am still obsessed with,” she says. “While I don’t typically wear fleeces with jeans, it’s a great way to make jeans and a white tee look fun while keeping it casual.”

If you’re looking for a button-front fleece, this Hit the Slopes version was recommended by trend forecasters, who called it a do-it-all jacket and highlighted its unique shade range. One expert described it as “reminiscent of a traditional teddy coat and an everyday-wear and activewear hybrid.”

Another outerwear option is the Pippa Packable Puffer, which was a top gift idea recommended by trend experts in 2022. Dubbed Free People’s “first-ever performance puffer,” it’s designed to fold into its own pocket and doubles as a travel pillow, Strategist writer Ambar Pardilla says. I also own this jacket, which is the ideal lightweight layer for errands or walks around my neighborhood in wet or cold conditions. I love that it’s loose-fitting while still feeling very insulating. This puffer comes in 20 colors, including Spice Tangerine and Sport Green.

While Campbell “Pookie” Puckett owns several matching pajama sets, she especially likes this one from Free People. “They’re so oversize and comfy. They don’t stick to your body, and they’re very flowy,” Puckett told us when we interviewed her about her favorite things. They also have a drawstring, and the wide leg is similar to a pair of sweatpants. “You just feel so good when you wear them,” she says. “I have a couple pairs, and I wear them at least a couple nights a week.”

Emily Hyland, the co-founder of the Pizza Loves Emily and Emmy Squared restaurants, told us she lives in this pull-on, low-back bralette. “It has a really thick band below it, which I think is really flattering for defined waistlines,” Hyland says. Hyland calls it the most comfortable bra and says she wears the ultra-stretchy style under everything.

When we stopped New Yorkers on the street to ask what work bags they were wearing around town, our staffers spotted three different people carrying the Free People Emerson bag. It received high praise for being made with durable textured leather, a roomy all-day capacity, and having many exterior and interior pockets for easy organization.

I own this sling bag in two shades, and I love that it’s super-functional (similar to Lululemon’s Everywhere Belt Bag) but with a dressier feel thanks to the suede and metal detailing. It’s ideal for travel or commuting to work because it’s roomy enough to hold essential belongings — including my wallet, keys, phone, charger, and sunglasses — while securely strapping across my chest. I also appreciate the tiny outer pocket for holding small items like lip balm and the side clip for easy-on, easy-off adjustments.

entry.title: What Hairstylist and Arey Co-Founder Jay Small Buys at the Drugstore
entry.summary: “It just transforms my morning.”
entry.content:
Here at the Strategist, we love hearing about everyday stuff that actually works. That line of thinking extends to the drugstore beauty products in our medicine cabinets, shower caddies, and makeup bags. In our series “Beauty Aisle,” we talk to folks in the beauty industry — aestheticians, hairstylists, makeup artists, dermatologists, and the like — about the go-to affordable products they keep stocked. For this installment, Strategist beauty writer Krista Bennett DeMaio chatted with Jay Small, co-founder of Arey, trichologist, and celebrity hairstylist, about the products her loves at the drugstore.

It’s just a classic and my go-to, whether it’s for my own personal use or when I’m behind the chair with clients. You really can’t overuse it. It’s a very flexible hair spray. You’ll never get that stiff or crunchy feeling. I can use it during an eight-hour shoot and keep changing the hair. That’s the beauty of this product. It also has a fragrance that’s very nostalgic. It reminds me of my mom.

I like this for all my male clients. It’s not too sticky or stiff, and you have time to manipulate it. I can work it through my hair with my hands, and then when it dries, it gets a little firm and holds the style in place.

It has a five-star rating. I buy this for anyone in my life, from my 10-year-old daughter to my hair assistants, because if I see them using it improperly, it doesn’t give me heart palpitations. I’ve given Mason Pearsons before, and they do not respect that it’s a $300 brush.

Honestly, it’s the tin. I like the way it looks. I’ve always been drawn to the aesthetic of the product and then the smell. I’ve always loved Carmex in the little jar, too, but now I can’t find it that way. So it’s Rosebud Salve for me.

I never thought of sea salt as a hand-cream ingredient, so this one caught my attention. It also has shea butter and argan oil. It absorbs pretty quickly. And if my hair is staticky and dry in the winter, I use some on my hair. A little hand cream goes a long way.

One thing to know about me is that I’m a dendrite, which means I take my oral hygiene incredibly seriously. That’s because I didn’t for a long time and I had to go through a whole series of dental treatments just to get to a normal baseline. So Dessert Essence Tea Tree Oil at Whole Foods is my go-to — because cavities don’t start on the surface of your teeth; they start in between your teeth. I literally get out of bed and floss my teeth and then do it multiple times a day. I like the fact that it’s waxed and not a ribbon, which may slide in between the teeth better, but it doesn’t take anything out. It also has tea-tree oil, so it stimulates your gums a little bit. It feels super clean.

When I look at it, I think man. But it has 48-hour protection, and it actually works. Not that I’ve ever put it to the 48-hour test. And it has charcoal, so it just feels like, Yes, this is doing something.

I love bar soaps. I get this one at Target. I love the smell of lavender. It just transforms my morning. I’m not big on bodywashes or loofahs. It feels like they’re encapsulating all the germs from yesterday.

This is a constant repurchase. My daughter uses them. They’re soft and easy on the hair, and they stretch out a lot.

entry.title: Save These Black Friday Deals Now, Shop Them Later
entry.summary: Everything we predict will be on sale during the biggest sale event of the year.
entry.content:
Black Friday is a little over three weeks away — it’s on November 27 this year — but lots of deals will begin much earlier. While we can’t guarantee any sale that’s not yet announced, our wealth of knowledge from years past means we have a strong idea of the upcoming discounts, including which retailers are likely to have their biggest sales of the year.

I combed through last year’s sales and several of our Best in Class lists to round up 100-ish items in a variety of categories that will probably drop in price over the next few weeks. If you see something you like and want to stay in the loop, click the heart icon next to any product to save it to your New York Magazine account. That way, you can easily check back on the prices of those items once Black Friday is here. Or you can sign up to receive emails when a product you’ve saved goes on sale — that way, you don’t have to scroll endlessly.

Before you start, check out senior deals editor Sam Daly’s guide to shopping Black Friday for a ton of useful tips and advice (and a few more product recommendations).

Pricey makeup, skin care, and hair care are often steeply discounted during Black Friday. Big retailers like Nordstrom, Sephora, Ulta, and Amazon will have the widest variety of products on sale. But be sure to check your favorite brands’ websites, too, as those could better than the big-box stores. (And often, they’ll throw in a free product with purchase.)

A lot of our favorite fashion brands have their best sales of the year during Cyber Week, including J.Crew, Gap, Madewell, Everlane, and Rothy’s. These discounts are a little harder to predict, as there will be truly thousands of items on sale, but you can safely assume most clothing brands will have sitewide discounts. For now, though, I kept my picks below to some of our favorite always-available items from some of our favorite brands. As with all sales, it’s a good time to stock up on basics like underwear and socks.

Mattress sales go live early and usually stay the same through Cyber Monday. Our best overall mattress, the Saatva Classic, is already discounted (though it might drop more), as is Avocado’s ecofriendly one. For bedding sales, Brooklinen, Cozy Earth, and Boll & Branch make some of my favorites — and bundles are usually at their best prices in November.

Another good area to splurge: Expensive cookware and appliances are often on sale during the weeks leading up to Thanksgiving. Some of my favorite brands to shop around this time are Strategist favorites Great Jones and Our Place. (Caraway already has deals on cookware sets.) Furniture from retailers like Article and Anthropologie typically go on sale well before Black Friday, too.

A lot of unsexy basics and household helpers go on sale, from batteries to water flossers. Expensive-but-worth-it luggage from brands like Away, Quince, and Hulken will also be deeply discounted (and makes a great gift). And if you’ve been contemplating a new vacuum, now’s the time.

Our tech writer Jordan McMahon says Black Friday is best for big-ticket items like TVs, Apple products, and fancy headphones. I’d wager that a few fitness and health trackers, like Oura Rings and Apple Watches, will also have nice sales, especially on older (but still useable) models.

Lastly, a ton of toys are set to go on sale from favorite brands including LEGO, Magna-Tiles, Melissa & Doug, and more. The same clothing retailers that’ll feature adult sales will likely also have a bunch of discounts for kids’ clothes — check Gap and Hanna Andersson. For babies, Lalo’s best-selling adpatable high chairs are already 20 percent off.

entry.title: How to Shop Black Friday and Cyber Monday, According to Our Deals Editor
entry.summary: A cheat sheet to navigating the best sales of the year.
entry.content:
Black Friday and Cyber Monday are without a doubt the best days of the year for sales. I should know — I write about sales all year long. Many retailers offer a 20 percent discount here and there throughout the year, but Black Friday is when they really let loose and increase that discount to 30 or 40 percent in a bid for your attention at the shoppiest time of all. If you approach these sales smartly, you can get all of your holiday shopping done early and below budget — and don’t forget about treating yourself.

Black Friday 2026 takes place on November 27, and runs through Monday, November 30, so you have some time to prepare. Sometimes it pays to shop early, before things sell out. Other times it pays to wait for a slightly better discount to come around. To help you navigate the sales, I’ve racked my deals-obsessed brain to come up with a list of tips, including which categories have the best deals, which you can safely skip, which deals tend to sell out fastest, and more.

Last year, we made it possible to save products on our site and see them in your account. I’d use that tool to start making your shopping list now. That way, when Black Friday rolls around, you can simply go to your account, see what’s on sale, and shop from there. Even better: Sign up for email notifications when something you’ve saved goes on sale. Black Friday sales often start long before the actual day, so the earlier you start saving products, the earlier you can start saving money.

One of my recently saved products, which I’m hoping will go on sale for Black Friday, is hydrating shower oil. (Crucial for winter!) “Along with its delicate floral scent, I love that the Bioderma has a gentle and fine lather, which washes away cleanly without any oily residue, so there’s no need to double-cleanse,” says writer Brenley Goertzen, who wrote our guide to the best bodywashes.

Shipping times are notoriously finicky this time of year, so it’s a good idea to order your gifts as early as possible. I suggest spending the weeks before Black Friday and Cyber Monday making a list of possible gifts for people on your list (and saving them to your account!), so when the sales go live, you can quickly check to see what’s on sale. And again, I’d do this sooner than later, as the deals have already started, and they’re already worth shopping.

If you need gift ideas, we’ve got plenty, and we’ll be finding all the best on-sale gifts now through Cyber Monday, so stay tuned for more. (I’d also recommend signing up for our Deal Freaks Daily newsletter, where we’ll be sharing all of our on-sale gift picks this holiday season.)

One year, I went into Black Friday shopping with the goal of finding the best deal I could on AirPod Pros. And find them I did, and for a respectable 24 percent off. It was one of only a few things I bought over the weekend.

Black Friday sales now begin early in November and ramp up through the month. For the most part, the deals that go live before Black Friday are the same as what you get during actual Cyber Week. There’s no way to be totally sure, but my rule of thumb: If the brand is smaller and calling the sale just a Black Friday or Cyber Week sale, it’s probably not going to change between now and Cyber Monday. If it’s a bigger retailer like Amazon and Nordstrom, and it’s calling the sale an early Black Friday sale (or something other than simply Black Friday), the deals probably will change closer to Black Friday. That doesn’t mean the early deals are bad; it’s just likely that new deals will be added to the mix.

All to say, in general, if there’s something you really want and it’s already on sale, get it while it’s in stock. If you don’t think the item will sell out, you can wait. There are a few cases where the deal is a bit better — like 25 percent off instead of 20 percent — come actual Black Friday.

Expensive items will be at their best prices on Black Friday — and shoppers no longer have to camp outside a JCPenney or Walmart in order to buy a washing machine or TV on sale. The deals have simply moved online, where you can find the best discounts of the year on appliances and tech. Best Buy and Target are both good places to start, especially if you’re looking for Apple tech or even a high-end vacuum. Some of these brands still have online doorbusters that only last a short amount of time, but they typically advertise them in advance, so you can plan ahead.

Our pick for the best noise-canceling headphones overall was on sale for October Prime Day for over $80 off. It should have a similar discount (if not slightly better) for Black Friday.

When people ask writer Jordan McMahon what they should wait to buy until Black Friday, his answer is always tech. Specifically, expensive tech like headphones, tablets, and gaming consoles. “You probably won’t find a better deal than the ones offered this week,” he says. Last year, we saw great deals at individual retailers like JBL, Sonos, and Dyson, as well as tons of discounts at such megaretailers as Best Buy, Amazon, and Target.

Tech is a category you should definitely check for price matching, though. Apple doesn’t discount its products on its own site, but it sometimes offers gift cards of varying amounts with the purchase of a product. Target, Best Buy, and Amazon, however, offer straight-up discounts on Apple products. The best place to buy depends on what you want — money now or later — but it’s worth comparing and considering before paying.

“Amazon always has significant discounts on its own products, like Kindles and Echo devices — I always wait until this time of year when I need to upgrade one of my e-readers,” McMahon says.

Sadly, the prices of streaming services just keep going up. Last year, we saw several streaming services offer more than half-off monthly subscription fees. If you’ve been unsure whether another streaming service is worth it, now is a good time to subscribe and try it out cheaply, often for a whole year. (These make a nice gift, too.)

As is usually the case during holiday sales, tons of clothes are significantly discounted. Last year, Madewell offered 40 percent off sitewide, and Alex Mill’s Black Friday sale was a surprise hit with Strategist readers and staffers alike. The sheer volume can be a bit overwhelming, though, which is why our senior fashion writer Ambar Pardilla will be sniffing out what’s actually a good deal. As she’s done in years past, she’ll be rounding up her best finds, organized by retailer, making it easy to compare discounts and find the very best ones.

One category I look forward to in the fashion sphere each Black Friday is the on-sale cashmere, and I’m sure this time around will be no diffferent.

According to senior writer Liza Corsillo, the big three — Amazon, Target, and Walmart — have the most sprawling deals on toys during Black Friday. Last year, she found dozens of options for over 50 percent off at these stores. But don’t limit yourself to just those three: Smaller, independent brands like Fat Brain Toys and Maisonette, for instance, had good (and sometimes even better) discounts, too, with up to 60 or 70 percent off certain toys.

A lot of beauty brands discount products by up to 20 percent throughout the year, but they almost always bump that discount up to 25 or 30 percent off for Black Friday. “I always use it as an opportunity to stock up on my favorite beauty products, buy gifts for loved ones, and try out new products I’ve been eyeing throughout the year,” says beauty writer Tembe Denton-Hurston. It’s a particularly good time to shop at Sephora: Last year, it offered up to 50 percent off brands like Augustinus Bader, Glossier, and Verb, and there were flash deals that changed daily. Also good to grab? Stocking stuffers like lip gloss, nail polish, and pimple patches.

Mattresses are always on sale. While a typical discount at any given time is about 15 to 20 percent off, Black Friday seems to be one of the only times mattress brands bump up the savings, usually by an extra 5 percent. (Those deals usually start well before Black Friday, so you don’t have to wait to get a better price.)

Retailers like Amazon, Nordstrom, and Target will often price-match the deals going on at other sites. This can make shopping easier because they’ll generally have faster and cheaper shipping and/or a more flexible return window, which is especially great for gift returns.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales vary from brand to brand, but in my experience, most places don’t increase discounts on Cyber Monday. At most, they might throw in a freebie with your purchase or add more items to the sales bin, but usually the discount is the same. So my advice here is the same as what I offered above: If you really want something, buy it early. If you’re willing to gamble on stock, you can wait and see if a discount changes or a freebie is added to the mix.

Yes, all the big brands will have sales, but so do smaller businesses — and they often don’t wait for Small Business Saturday to go live. Salter House never has sales, but I bought this nightdress while it was a rare 20 percent off on Black Friday a few years ago.

If this year is anything like the past few, a fair amount of retailers will extend their sales and turn the entire first week of December into a full-on Cyber Week. The discounts won’t change from Cyber Monday, but brands might throw in a free gift with purchase to persuade you to check out.

entry.content:
It’s rare to see a sitewide sale at Sephora, so the Savings Event is an exciting time. From now until November 9, the entire site is discounted at varying levels based on your reward tier. The discounts are best at the highest tier, Rouge, which gets you 20 percent off the entire site. This requires a spend of $1,000 in a calendar year. The biggest change this year is that for the first time, Rouge members can share their discount, extending 20 percent off to five friends. The next level, VIB, requires a spend of at least $350 a year and results in 15 percent off. Finally there’s Insider, which only requires an email sign-up. Everyone is eligible for 30 percent off of Sephora Collection, the brand’s in-house line that’s beloved by Sephora employees and Strategist writers both. There are thousands of products to choose from, so I’ve gone through and selected a mix of things we’ve written about before.

Those, below.

One of the few sunscreens with the new FDA-approved filter, bemotrizinol or BEMT, this hybrid sunscreen has a lightweight texture and a matte finish.

We named these exfoliating peel pads the best exfoliator peels on the market. Writer Arielle Avila says that, while pricey, they’re worth it: “After just one night of using this, my skin looks bright and silky smooth the next day.”

Writer Erin Stovall went through 120 moisturizers before landing on this one from Tatcha, which she says moisturizes her dry skin but still sits nicely under makeup. It’s both plumping and hydrating thanks to a blend of squalane, hyaluronic acid, Japanese purple rice, and red algae.

These icy toner-filled pods hang out in the freezer until they’re ready to use. Each one contains brightening niacinamide, moisturizing glycerin, and soothing green tea, which work together to support the skin’s barrier and brighten over time. Playwright Jeremy O. Harris swears by them. “The minute I take [the pods] away, I look at my face, and it feels tighter, like my skull got closer to my skin in a really nice way. It’s drooping less,” he says.

Also available from Sofie Pavitt is the Omega moisturizer, which is beloved by esthetician and writer Rio Viera-Newton as well as senior editor Hilary Reid, who is on her third jar. “The formula feels luxuriously dense when you rub it into your skin but hasn’t caused any breakouts,” she says.

I’m a longtime fan of this hypochlorous acid from Tower28, which helps to keep my skin breakout free and calm, especially after going to the gym and being in the sun.

If there’s one thing I’ll be buying during the sale, it’s this moisturizer. It’s nourishing and soothing — even my most irritated skin is calmed by a dollop of cream. Actress Miriam Petche is also a fan. “Whenever my skin is deciding to be dramatic, this calms it down,” she says.

Actress Ariana DeBose swears by this lip balm, which is packed with peptides and vitamin C. Together the ingredients smooth fine lines and plump up the skin.”I feel like this lip balm makes my lips luscious,” she says.

Also on the lip front, it’s a good opportunity to stock up on the beloved Laneige Lip Sleeping Mask, a Strategist staple. Most recently, it came recommended by Olivia Jade, who said it’s the only lip balm that actually hydrates.

When we polled Strategist readers on their favorite body washes, this truly excellent one from Necessaire took the crown. It lathers and makes you feel clean but doesn’t strip the skin, and it comes in a range of nice-smelling scents.

entry.title: The Best Highball Glasses, According to Bartenders
entry.summary: For your gin-and-tonics, rum-and-Cokes, and other two-ingredient cocktails.
entry.content:
Gin-and-tonic, whisky (or rum)–and-Coke, Scotch-and-soda: These are just a few examples of the single-liquor cocktail known as a “highball,” which is served in a tall, narrow, straight-sided glass of the same name. Highball glasses (also called hi-ball or Collins glasses, as in the cocktail Tom Collins) are intended for larger-volume drinks with a ratio of two (or sometimes three) ounces of mixer to one ounce of spirit. They hold lots of ice to slowly dilute the liquor.

You would generally look for a simple, clear highball glass that’s roughly six inches tall and two or three inches wide and that holds about eight to 12 ounces. A range of options fits that description. For this guide, I spoke to a dozen bartenders about their favorites. While handwashing with hot, soapy water is preferable for these thinner, more delicate glasses, I have included a couple that are dishwasher safe. If you’re looking for other essential barware, we also have guides to the best coupe glasses, cocktail strainers, and cocktail muddlers.

Updated on November 4, 2026
All our highball recommendations below have been updated with the latest pricing and availability.

This glass’s curved bottom gives it a distinctive look. It comes recommended by Michael McCaulley, beverage director at Schulson Collective in Philadelphia. “It is the perfect size and has a sleek shape and a contoured texture that feels great in your hand. The rim is thin (which helps with effortless sipping), and the weight is just right,” he says. “It’s a good Goldilocks size — neither too small nor too large. The glass is faceted so it catches the light well in the bar.”

Jordan Deis at the Saint-Germain wine bar in New Orleans looks for versatility in his glassware and swears by these Duralex glasses. “They’re reasonably priced and durable and boast a classic design that elevates the presentation of any drink,” says Deis, who uses these tumblers for highballs, sodas, or even water and juices. The Picardie line comes in various sizes, but opt for 12 ounces or higher for highballs. They’re a bit thicker, and therefore stronger, than the ordinary highball glass, and they’re stackable for convenient storage as well as dishwasher safe.

If you’ve ever wanted to re-create the ambiance of a nice hotel bar at home, these glasses run a little on the pricey side but are “beautifully crafted and have an amazing look and feel,” says Ricardo Rodriguez, beverage director of New Jersey’s Lita and its cocktail bar, La Otra. He prefers thin and minimalist highball glasses for a Scandinavian design aesthetic.

To use at home, Kraig Rovensky, owner of the Seattle bar Life on Mars, prefers the Japanese brand Usuhari’s glasses. “They’re incredibly thin, light, and durable,” he says. “Generally, I find Usuhari highball glasses work best with a cocktail that’s a little bit of a showman: tall and colorful with great garnishes and some crushed ice.”

Jason Kaminski is an avid vintage-barware collector and caterer who appreciates upcycled glassware. Mixed drinks are one of the biggest requests at his events, and in his line of work, he expects highball glasses to break. So buying dishwasher-safe glassware on a budget is important. He loves these Remark cups, made in Philadelphia from discarded kombucha bottles, for higher-quality highball glasses. “They’re easy to hold, especially when you’re standing for hours at a cocktail event, and are slim enough not to take up too much cabinet space,” he says. “They also don’t take up a lot of table space and can be easily placed next to the wineglasses.”

These Riedel crystal glasses have cool vertical ridges that make them visually appealing. They come recommended by Bar Bastion creative bar director Maxwell Britten, who likes their “elegant design, high-quality crystal construction, and excellent durability. They are perfect for showcasing the clarity and color of the drink while providing a sophisticated look,” he says. With these more expensive glasses, you should avoid harsh detergents that could damage the crystal. Britten advises drying them with a lint-free cloth to prevent water spots and storing them upright.

Adrienne Gomez-Saddler, bartender at the Four Seasons Philadelphia, also takes meticulous glassware care and storage seriously. “I enjoy a highball or Collins glass that has a clear finish for a drink with effervescence,” she says. She appreciates Riedel’s symmetrical design, which allows for “even sipping” — meaning you get a blend of both the spirit and the mixer with each sip, unlike with shaped glasses (martini, pilsner, or flutes) in which ingredients can settle at the bottom.

Tyler Chauvin, assistant general manager of food and beverage at Swingers, the Crazy Golf Club, recommends this option from Williams Sonoma for a classic home bar. “The sleek lines and slim shape give it a sexy aesthetic that is both modern and timeless,” she says. “The vertical weaved lines draw the eye up to the shape of the glass.” She uses highball glasses for drinks like mojitos or Dark and Stormys. The 16-ounce volume is a bit larger than the standard highball glass but works during the summer as the extra space allows for more ice.

Rollin Colmenares says a highball is the most used glass at the RT60 Rooftop Bar at the Hard Rock Hotel New York. He considers this JoyJolt Faye highball glass an essential piece of equipment for its midrange size and solid base. “They’re sturdier and harder to break, are comfortable to hold, contain a lot of volume, and allow the aromas of garnishes to be concentrated at the top,” he says. The small surface area also keeps drinks effervescent for much longer than a lowball would.

My Loup bar manager Jillian Moore needs a highball glass that can handle the “wear and tear of restaurant life” but that’s great for a range of drinks. “At My Loup, we use a basic Collins glass since it’s all-purpose and economical.” The lack of embellishment is key, she says, as “I like using ridiculous garnishes like silly straws, mini-clothespins, or disco-ball cocktail picks.”

Being economical is also a requirement for Hospitality HQ director of operations Steven Escobar. These Libbey Chicago glasses are “durable and inexpensive, have a nice shape, and work well as a specialty-cocktail glass,” he says.

Dean Hakim, bar manager at Heirloom @ the St. Laurent, is fond of Nude glassware because of the brand’s thin, durable highball glasses with solid bases. “They’re extremely elegant,” says Hakim. “They have gorgeous ridges in the glass, the height is tall, and the glass fits well in your hand.”

entry.title: I Found a Genuine Leather Skirt I Can Wear All Day
entry.summary: No faux here.
entry.content:
For back-to-work shopping this fall, I’ve been looking for a leather midiskirt to wear to the office. I rely heavily on my cotton and linen midiskirts in the summer and spring and realized my wardrobe could use a cool-weather counterpart. And while I don’t want to sound too much like a women’s magazine from the early aughts, I like the potential a leather skirt offers to easily transition from “day to night” — or at least from my desk to dinner plans.

My requirements are as follows: It has to be available in a size 12 or 14 (which can be tricky since leather doesn’t have as much stretch), midi length, and, while I’m open to different silhouettes, must be comfortable enough to walk and sit in. I’m not picky when it comes to color, but the skirt also has to be 100 percent genuine leather. No “vegan” leather allowed. As I’ve been browsing, it’s truly shocking what some brands want to charge these days for faux leather, which is typically made from polyurethane or PVC, but I’ve found many contenders that are not. Below, the ones that were almost there and the winners.

While I was pursuing Sézane’s new fall offerings, I found a treasure trove of leather-skirt options. While I initially wanted a straighter silhouette, I figured it wouldn’t hurt to give a more relaxed A-line skirt a try, since I have a nearly ten-inch difference between my waist and my hips and I thought the fit would be a bit less tricky. Unfortunately, I misjudged the sizing anyway and ordered the Soelle skirt in a size too large. I am happy to report that Sézane’s sizing is generous, but you might want to go down a size if you’re in between like I am. Even after I pinned it, I realized it was just too voluminous for the look I was going for — I felt like I was drowning in the fabric.

I really, really liked the look of the built-in belt on the brand’s Yasmin skirt, but once I tried the skirt on, I realized it wasn’t super-functional. And while I thought the skirt was going to be a rich chestnut brown, in person the leather was a much lighter shade than the product pictures showed on the website. The fit was better than the Soelle skirt above, but I realized I wanted something a bit more formfitting.

This led me to try on the Sézane Magalia, which is a column skirt. The Magalia did come in the richer shade of brown I was after, and I really liked the more figure-skimming cut, but I did notice some pulling around my stomach. Not a deal-breaker, and I will still happily wear this skirt out, but I think I could do better.

After striking out with the A-line skirts at Sézane, I didn’t have much hope for this burgundy number from Mint Velvet, but I was surprised by how much I liked it. Of the A-line skirts I tried on, it was by far my favorite. The skirt was full but I didn’t feel overwhelmed by the silhouette, and the rich burgundy color was gorgeous — it actually looked better in person than it did on the website.

The Elle Skirt from Thomas and Lourdes was almost perfect. The fit was fantastic, and the 100 percent lamb leather was supple and thick but not too constricting. However, the skirt did have a major pet peeve of mine: an exposed silver zipper. The zipper disrupts the skirt’s sleek, all-black design, and I wish it had been concealed in the seam so that the back panel remained smooth.

This was definitely one of the best-fitting skirts I tried. The leather itself was quite soft while still being tailored correctly (with an invisible zipper!), so it really hugged my body with no waist gapping. I also appreciated that there is a slit in the back that makes it easier to walk in. However, while this is a very comfortable pencil skirt, it is still a pencil skirt, and I can see myself wearing it more for events than to the office for a full day of sitting. But I am really looking forward to breaking this out for my calendar of holiday parties come December. The dark red is just right: festive, but not so Christmasy that it can’t also be worn the rest of the year.

I’ve been eyeing the A.L.C. Marta skirt since last fall, so I couldn’t wait to get my hands on it when it was brought back this season. The silhouette is a slightly more generous column design, so it gives me a bit more much-needed room through the hips while still fitting snugly at my waist. The leather is also the right weight — soft enough to lay nicely against the body but not so soft that it lacks structure. I also really loved the dark-brown shade I tried on that feels a bit warmer on my skin than true black, but it’s also available in dark red and black.

It probably comes as no surprise that the Tibi skirt was one of my favorites. The construction is different from all the other skirts on this list — true to its “trouser” name it has belt loops, a front zipper, and back pockets to resemble a pair of pants. I like the styling potential the belt loops add and it feels like this skirt has more versatility since it can be worn at either the high or mid waist. I also felt the most excited to style this skirt — it played well with others and looked equally great whether I added a blazer, sweater, or tee. If you’re looking for a true investment piece, this is the winner.

However, on the other end of the affordability spectrum, is this very nice option from Nordstrom, which also hit it out of the park. I was extremely impressed overall with the quality. It fits well with no pulling and sits somewhere between a pencil and a column skirt, so while it hugs my curves it isn’t so narrow that I can’t sit in it comfortably. While the leather is a bit thinner than the other skirts on this list, it looks just as good for half the price, which I think is a more than fair trade-off.

entry.summary: Plus the under-$25 gift I hope to find in my stocking.
entry.content:
I love a “nice” shirt as much as the next person. But after testing out so many to find worthwhile white tees under $100, I’m exhausted with the same batch of premium brands pushing the same kinds of premium tops. Release us from the shackles of Flore Flore, the boatneck, and the crew neck! Since my last dispatch, I’ve been focused on finding both plain basics and elevated staples from labels I’ve never heard of. Here’s what I’ve been loving.

I totally fell for a targeted ad for this New York–based label, and I’m so glad I did. I have a propensity for a high-neck top, and this henley with a twist scratched my different-type-of-basic itch with its monochrome poplin placket and stand collar. It’s the first time I’ve seen the style with seven buttons, my lucky number. Worn completely buttoned up, it’s more refined than a typical slouchy henley.

[Editor’s note: This top is currently out of stock, but you can sign up for restock notifications on the product page.]

I couldn’t be happier to have discovered Kye Intimates, a Los Angeles–based brand making tops and bottoms in the same vein of Flore Flore but with an intimatewear approach.  This three-quarter-sleeve top’s high V-neck beautifully frames the face and neck without feeling suffocating, and the piping along the neck and chest emphasizes its strong lines. I felt like I had nothing on in the best way when trying this: The jersey is like a second skin with plenty of stretch but complete opacity.

I recently popped into Mess in the West Village, a boutique stocking familiar favorites like Brooke Callahan alongside several lines I’d never heard of. Among them was By Signe, a Danish line making Flore Flore–like essentials from natural fibers such as organic cotton but a pinch more affordable (and more playfully printed). This tank came home with me; its silk trim is lovely. The striated ribbing adds a delicate texture and sufficient coverage, making it more of a top rather than just a tank.

Loyal as I am to my five-strong Boat and Tote collection, I’ve coveted a brightly colored, contrast-stitched Hèrmes Fourre Tout tote since I first discovered them on one of many aimless nights spent scrolling the RealReal. I have sifted through eBay, Poshmark, and Vestiaire Collective on and off over the past six months but have yet to find the right color, size, condition, and price point. However, I might’ve discovered something even better in these Field bags, which evoke the Fourre Tout in so many ways and can be endlessly stuffed (the snaps on the sides of the bag allow it to expand). I’ve tried both the Classic and Mini sizes, and the latter is perfect as a daily tote: I used it to schlep a laptop, a planner, paperwork, a water bottle, and snacks while reporting uptown last week.

I’m always pondering the going-out-top quandary. And I’m still fixated on this summer’s look, a deep racerback tank. This one from Orseund Iris, a gorgeous “your Hanes tank but better,” has lived in my head for weeks, and I indeed fell hard after trying it on. Think of it as the even fancier counterpart to By Signe’s April. I recently visited friends on the West Coast and packed this top with me; it was the perfect base for evenings out at swankier dinners. The thick silk trim coupled with the shoulder-blade-baring wide-set back is daring and elegant without showing too much.

I didn’t know about Morjas until I spotted the brand’s sneakers on the feet of a gentleman in Chelsea while reporting on shoes. Browsing the brand’s site later, I found every leather boot, pump, and flat more handsome than the last. These shoes remind me of my Chanel flats — just as elongated and low vamped in shape and form but more sculpted. A stitched border around the opening frames the foot beautifully, and just a pinch of toe cleavage peeks through. I got them in an espresso brown leather, a welcome change from black, and have been doing my best to resist the ivory and ruby.

My love for spicy noodles knows no bounds, and Arih’s recently appeared on my radar. I’m curious to try the wide range of flavors I’ve never seen in instant-noodle form before: spicy seaweed, truffle bulgogi, gochujang butter …

My OXO bottle stoppers are plenty useful but not cute enough. This one’s a part of Areaware’s latest relaunch, and there’s nothing more me than Yves Klein blue glass. I think it would make for a great under-$25 stocking stuffer.

High up on my holiday wish list is some new gold. I’m pondering a solitaire diamond bezel bracelet (or a few): Lindsey Leigh’s are delightfully delicate, and I was surprised how much I love the look of a singular pinprick stone on the first pick. It catches the light subtly with no shortage of shimmer. From Vrai, I’m enjoying the variety of shapes on offer. I’m very into the idea of building a trio stack in different cuts — round, baguette, and oval.
