entry.title: How 8 Women Get Their Gray Hair to Look So Good
entry.summary: We asked women to share their silver-hair-care secrets.
entry.content:
I recently wrote about trying Arey, a line of products designed to help prevent or slow the appearance of gray hair. I only have a few grays, and for now, I’m happy to be doing something to prevent them. But I also have a friend, makeup artist Marie D’Onofrio, whose naturally grown-in silver hair makes me reconsider that position every time I see her. She has long, thick, wavy gray hair with a beautiful silver section around her face that looks like a money piece, a face-framing highlight. People stop her all the time to ask about it and tell her how gorgeous it is.

I may not be ready to embrace gray strands yet, but I am curious about what it takes to get there. Is the grow-out as awkward as I imagine it would be? Does your hair’s texture change? Which products do you use to keep the gray looking bright? Do you need to rethink your makeup? And what does it feel like to finally stop worrying about your roots?

I asked eight women who have embraced their natural gray to share their experiences. Some went cold turkey, while others worked with a colorist, and their timelines ranged from about a year to several years. Their approaches to hair care and makeup are just as individual. Here’s how they got there, what they’ve learned, and the products they rely on now.

D’Onofrio, 43, decided to go gray back in November 2020. “At the time, I was doing a single process every week and a half to two weeks, and my hair was becoming resistant to color,” she says. To test the waters, she bought a gray wig and posted a picture on social media. “The feedback was insane!” It was the push she needed. “I ended up cutting my hair into a bob to make it a little easier, and I lightened the front to help blend my natural gray.” She says the process wasn’t easy. “It took about two years to get to a place where I love my hair.”

Marie has a few tricks for keeping her silver bright. Once a week, she washes with Clairol Shimmer Lights Shampoo and follows with Joico Color Balance Purple Conditioner. Every other month, she uses two professional glazes: Joico Vero K-PAK Color Intensity in clear and lavender. “The glaze helps tone the gray, neutralize any yellowing from environmental factors, styling, and product buildup, and my hair feels softer and shinier.” She also protects her hair when heat styling, particularly with Color Wow Dream Coat.

She’s learned that makeup matters, too. “I find myself wearing more blush and incorporating brighter colors like purple or turquoise eyeliner.”

“I’ve been openly gray for the past 11 years,” says Evelyn Wang, but she started finding grays in her teens and dyed her hair for years, beginning in her 20s. For a long time, she thought about going gray: “I was definitely tired of the hair-dye process, which was becoming a more frequent part of my life.” She even had a secret Pinterest board of aspirational silver-haired women. “When I finally decided to do it, I took an indirect route and first went blonde, then eventually gray-blended.” Going fully gray took about two years.

The experience also gave her a new appreciation for the specific needs of gray hair and eventually inspired her to create Silverist because she couldn’t find the exact routine she wanted for her own hair. “I also realized how much more buildup shows on lighter hair,” she says. “Think about how easily you see a stain on a white T-shirt.” She designed the Clarity Reset Demineralizer, a pre-shampoo treatment, to remove buildup from minerals, metals, and chlorine that can leave hair looking dull or discolored. She also uses the Lustrous Rituals Buildable Tone Shampoo, which isn’t a purple shampoo. “It gives a lighter, more subtle dose of toning to help with vibrancy without overwhelming your natural color.”

Like D’Onofrio, Wang’s makeup routine has evolved, too. She used to love a nude lip — she grew up in the “M.A.C Spice era,” as she describes it — but now finds that brighter reds, pinks, and fuchsias give her complexion more life. She also pays closer attention to applying makeup around her hairline, since it shows more against her lighter hair.

Trae Bodge let her grays grow in her mid-20s. “I was working at Kiehl’s at the time, and I remember that older women, especially older Black women, were quite upset that I was allowing my gray streaks to come in,” she says. “They told me it aged me and I should dye it ASAP.” She didn’t listen and let the gray come through.

In her 40s, she found that her hair was a bit too gray and began adding lowlights that matched her original hair color, making it appear less gray overall. Now that her hair is becoming increasingly white, she has started using Overtone Color-Depositing Conditioner to darken it by a shade or two. “The rinses work well, but I’ve learned the hard way that you can’t combine them with the purple brightening shampoos because you can end up with a color that doesn’t look right,” she says. “My hair turned a bit greenish in a few spots.” It took some experimentation to get it back to the right shade. “Not ideal when you’re on TV a lot.” Otherwise, she uses Potion Studio shampoo and conditioner.

Bodge’s naturally curly hair texture brings another challenge. The gray around her temples is softer than the rest of her hair, and when she stretches her curls with a blow-dryer, she has to be careful not to overdo it. Too much heat can leave those sections limp and straighter than the rest. Her go-to leave-in conditioner is Cantu Moisturizing Curl Activator Cream. She uses the Ecoslay Orange Marmalade Curl Definer to freshen up her curls between washes, Dippity Do Girls Curl Gelee to tame frizz, and Slickhair Slick Stick for her edges.

She’s also noticed her brows become grayer and sparser. She uses a Renata Spot Tint Kit and Lavone Eyebrow Pomade to add definition. Her makeup colors have shifted, too. “I used to wear a lot of warm tones, and now cooler tones look much better on me, especially lips and cheeks.” She says the same is true of her wardrobe. “I can get away with cool, bright colors much more than I used to.”

For Pati Dubroff, a celebrity makeup artist, the decision to go gray came after a major health event. “The real impetus was having brain surgery,” she says. She had been coloring her hair since her late 30s, and she couldn’t dye it for three to four months while she recovered. She and her friend and hairstylist Chris McMillan decided to cut her long, dyed-brown hair and start working toward gray.

It wasn’t a quick process. She was completely gray by age 49. They cut off a significant amount of length and tried lightening her hair to blonde. “That first day in the salon was about seven hours!” she recalls. “It took a couple of years before it started to feel like a cool-toned silver.” Dubroff still visits the salon about three times a year for balayage with colorist Lien at Chris McMillan Salon. “The goal is to weave more gray through the darker hair in the back, brighten the front, and keep the overall tone cool,” she says. “Now I’m just thrilled with my long gray hair.”

To keep it vibrant, she uses AGEbeautiful Brightening Wash and the Deep Conditioning Hair Mask. (Dubroff is a spokesperson for the brand.) RŌZ Foundation Mask is another favorite for keeping her hair healthy and nourished. Chris McMillan’s the Glassy Smooth Hair Oil is a fine mist that she uses to make her ends smooth and vibrant.

The makeup artist has learned that brows are especially important with gray hair. “My brows are still a light brunette, but I use a brow pencil that’s more of a cool, dark blonde, very taupe with no warmth at all,” she says. “I don’t want my brows to look too severely dark, so I go a little lighter and cooler when filling in.” She also likes more blush and creamy bronzer to bring warmth and contrast to her complexion. 

Michelle LeVasseur, a.k.a. “Meesh,” had wanted to go gray for years, but her hairdresser kept talking her out of it. She was told she was too old, that her color wouldn’t suit her, and that her husband wouldn’t like it. “The beauty world had always taught us that forever young meant beautiful and that gray meant old and ugly, so I kept dyeing,” she says.

The decision finally came in October 2024, after she returned from a family trip to Puerto Rico with COVID. She didn’t have the energy to get to the salon for another root touch-up, so she decided to stop coloring altogether.
“The first few months were the hardest,” she says. In the beginning, a round patch of gray at her crown made her reach for baseball caps and beanies. By month three, she felt like nothing was happening. By month four, the line between her natural roots and colored lengths was becoming more obvious. She heard comments from people who thought gray would make her look old, as well as compliments from others. But even being called “brave” didn’t sit quite right with her: “Why should growing out your grays be considered scary?”

Around month ten, Michelle found a hairdresser who was also growing out her gray. A haircut helped the color look more blended. At the one-year mark, her gray had reached her ears. “I finally threw out the box dye and the root touch-up powder.”

Now, at 56, she says “gray is just another color.” Sharing her journey online helped hold her accountable to her process but also gave others permission. “I’m not here to tell women to go gray; I’m here to show them what it can look like, so they can decide for themselves.”

Her hair-care routine includes using Aveda Botanical Repair Purple Toning Shampoo about once a month to brighten her silver. She’s also become more aware of how water quality can affect the look and feel of her hair, so she uses Silverist Clarity Reset Demineralizer Pre-Shampoo, too. She likes long layers for movement and to show off the natural pattern of her gray.

After 35 years in the beauty industry, Claudia Fabian was ready to stop coloring her roots every two weeks. She decided to embrace her gray in October 2020. She didn’t want to cut her hair short to make the transition faster, so she let it grow. The process took four years. She describes it as like “watching paint dry” and says the early months can look a little like you’ve missed a hair appointment. It gets easier after about six months, she says, and she actually loved the in-between stage when gray roots met the remaining colored lengths.

Her advice to anyone considering it is to give the process time. She uses the phrase “it takes a year to your ear” to describe how long it can take before the gray has grown down far enough to feel like a real change. And while it’s easy to feel self-conscious during the awkward stage, she reminds women that no one else cares. “I can’t imagine coloring my hair ever again,” she says. “It would be like covering up beautiful hardwood floors with ugly shag carpet.”

Fabian doesn’t believe gray hair automatically requires purple shampoo or a special makeup routine. She chooses shampoo and conditioner based on her hair type and texture. She likes the brand Back of the Bottle and uses purple conditioner only every few months if she feels her hair needs it. She also cautions that toning products can be drying when overused.

Fabian has not let her gray hair dictate the rest of her style. “I do not subscribe to the antiquated rules put upon women over 50,” she says. “I have my hair long and I wear it in a long-layered cut.”

Lynn Shabinsky stopped coloring her hair at 46 after more than 20 years of dyeing it. She was tired of touching up her roots every two weeks, and her reasoning was straightforward: “If men could do it, so could I!”

She quit hair dye cold turkey, though she did use a temporary rinse for a few weeks before deciding to stop that, too. Her transition was relatively easy compared to some of the others. She already had blonde highlights, and her roots were about 90 percent white, so the difference between her natural color and the rest of her hair wasn’t as dramatic. It took about a year to grow out completely. “It was quite liberating!” she says. “I felt free!”

Her approach to hair care has become simpler over time. She initially experimented with purple and blue shampoos but learned that some products could contribute to discoloration. Now she sticks with gentle shampoo from SEEN, minimal styling products, and occasionally uses Amika Bust Your Brass Shampoo, conditioner, and hair mask when she wants to brighten her color. Shabinsky air-dries before styling with lower heat, wears a hat in the sun, and uses a rich cream or oil when her hair feels dry or frizzy.

Revelina Tokromo noticed her first gray hairs in her early 20s. There were so few that she could count them, so she simply plucked them out. By 34 or 35, she had become noticeably grayer and started dyeing her hair black. In 2014, Tokromo lost her hair while undergoing chemotherapy, and it grew back gray.

In September 2017, she stopped dyeing her hair, and she has never regretted the decision. “I truly believe the key is to own your gray hair with confidence,” she says. Her hair is an extension of who she is now, and she reminds herself, “Growing older is a privilege.”

The process took about a year. Tokromo uses Olaplex No. 4P Blond Enhancer Purple Toning Shampoo and No. 5P purple toning conditioner to help neutralize yellow tones, along with salon-quality conditioner and hair oil for shine and softness. She styles it with a Revlon Volumizing Air Brush to create loose, beachy waves, and occasionally visits the salon for an intensive keratin treatment.

entry.title: The Best Emergency Radios, According to Disaster-Preparedness Experts
entry.summary: They’re an essential part of any emergency-preparedness kit.
entry.content:
You may not think you need an emergency radio since you can get weather reports and news from your cell phone or TV. During emergencies like a hurricane or earthquake or terrorist attack, however, when power and Wi-Fi may be out and cell towers may be down, an emergency radio can be a vital backup source of information, as well as of power, light, and even entertainment. “Diversifying your technology ecosystem to be able to receive the alert two, three, maybe even four times is a great way to make sure that you can protect yourself and your family,” says Andrew Phelps, COO of AC Disaster Consulting and the former head of emergency management for the state of Oregon.

Besides Phelps, we spoke to many survival and emergency preparedness experts to find out what to look for in an emergency radio. They told us a good one can be charged in multiple ways, and should have at minimum a flashlight and AM/FM radio, in addition to weather band channels, which broadcast weather alerts in a localized area. Other helpful features include a beacon, SOS alarm, and USB ports for charging devices. Some models have Bluetooth connectivity, so you can stream music from other devices, or shortwave radio as another information source.

National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration updates can be found in the 162.400 to 162.550 MHz frequency band — you can look online to get the exact frequencies for your area. Radios with a Public Alert or NOAA All Hazards logo automatically play updates from the NOAA without having to be turned on, while models with the SAME designation can be programmed to issue alerts for a specific area. Alerts from other emergency services generally go out through AM and FM commercial broadcast stations — that’s the Emergency Alert System you might hear being tested from time to time. The AM band tends to have news stations, while FM stations such as NPR affiliates can be a good source for general news.

Each of our expert picks has a rechargeable battery that can be powered by a USB connection, hand crank, and solar panel. Some also take disposable batteries. The power generated by hand cranks varies depending on the radio, but a minute of cranking might power a radio for about ten minutes — just enough time to catch important updates. The USB ports on the radios can be used to recharge devices such as cell phones or tablets. If you think you might need to use your radio for an extended period of time or to charge devices, Mykel Hawke, a former U.S. Army special-forces captain and author of several survival books, suggests looking for an emergency radio with a battery that holds at least 4,000 mAh of battery capacity.

Stephanie Fox, national spokesperson for the American Red Cross, says there are three basic tenets to emergency preparedness: “Build a kit, have a plan, and stay informed.” That means just having a radio isn’t enough; to be truly prepared, make sure the radio is fully charged and set to the appropriate stations if needed before an emergency, and that you have spare batteries nearby if it takes them.

To help you find the best emergency radio that you hopefully won’t ever have to use, we asked preppers, survivalists, first responders, and the merely well-prepared what emergency radio models they use and recommend to family and friends.

Updated on November 3, 2026
These radios have been updated with the latest availability and pricing.

Many experts we spoke to recommended Kaito radios, which have features like extra-sensitive antennas and crisp speakers. This model offers Bluetooth connectivity, so you can stream music from other devices, and short-wave radio, which can be helpful in non-weather emergencies. Shortwave-band signals bounce off the atmosphere and can travel long distances, so if you’re in a situation where all nearby communication is cut off — a coup, for example, or an earthquake that knocks out radio towers — you might be able to pick up a radio broadcast from another part of the world that offers updates on the situation in your area. “In an extreme global situation, an entire country may be off-grid, but someone, somewhere, will be broadcasting,” says Thomas Coyne, the owner and lead instructor at Thomas Coyne Survival Schools. Along with a 600-mAh rechargeable battery, the Kaito KA500 can be charged by AA batteries. It can be set to receive weather alerts and, says survivalist EJ. “Skullcrusher” Snyder, whom you might know from his many appearances on Naked and Afraid, “It has a five-LED reading lamp, LED flashlight, and red LED SOS beacon light.”

Jim Cobb, author of Prepper’s Home Defense and The Prepper’s Complete Book of Disaster Readiness, calls the Kaito Voyager Max KA900 a “great option” that’s “intuitive and easy to use.” It offers a lot of bells and whistles, including digital tuning and a backlit display, and is an excellent choice if you’re going to use it both as an everyday radio and an emergency system (like the KA500, it receives AM/FM and shortwave signals). It has better sound quality than smaller radios thanks to the stereo speakers and 14-inch antenna, and there’s a built-in system for recording radio broadcasts. Bluetooth connectivity and an audio-input jack also allow you to stream your own music. “The crank and solar options are not incredibly efficient, but they work well enough,” Cobb says, and the 2,000-mAh battery can also be charged with a wall power adapter that’s purchased separately.

Phelps gives Midland radios high marks for being “really durable” and easy to figure out how to use right out of the box. Nat, known as the Preparedness Guy and host of a prepper podcast, has been using Midland radios for years. He says the company’s ER310 is a solid option, as is the ER210, which has slightly fewer features. Both radios have two key features he looks for: a flashlight (“a must”) and a backlit display screen (“nice to have”). In addition, the ER310 has an emergency beacon, weather-alarm capabilities, and an ultrasonic dog whistle, which sends out a call to rescuers if you’re lost in the woods. Along with a 2,600-mAh rechargeable battery, it can be charged with AA batteries.

Pete, the Texas-based survivalist behind the YouTube channel the Roaming Prepper, who prefers to use only his first name, throws this radio in a carry-on bag when he’s traveling and leaves it on the nightstand at whatever hotel he’s staying at. He recommends city dwellers pack a compact model like this — this one weighs less than a pound but still packs in a flashlight, reading light, and SOS alarm — in their work bags. If you’re sitting at your desk and experience an emergency like a terrorist attack or a blackout, “You can pop it on and start getting information,” he says, even if cell-phone lines are jammed. Having real-time updates helps you start forming a plan, including whether to evacuate and where to go. This radio has a relatively small internal battery (2,000 mAh) but can be charged with AAA batteries.

Hawke gives this radio high marks for its 10,000-mAh battery, which will allow you to power more devices or keep your radio running longer than the less-powerful batteries of the other models on this list. This model can be programmed to receive NOAA alerts and also features a flashlight, SOS alarm, alarm clock, and headphone jack.

Pete recommends this model from Eton, which sends out a notice whenever there’s a new weather alert from the NOAA. His Eton was “going off all night” when Hurricane Harvey hit in 2017. With cell service down, he believes many of the fatalities associated with the storm were caused by people not knowing what was going on or trying to drive through flooded streets. It has a 2,600 mAh battery, Bluetooth connectivity, a digital tuner and display, a flashlight, and an emergency beacon. The panel light also works well as a camping lantern.

entry.title: The 10 Very Best Weighted Blankets
entry.summary: “They feel like being swaddled or held in a firm hug.”
entry.content:
If you struggle with falling (and staying) asleep, a weighted blanket can be a useful accessory to help you enjoy a better night’s slumber. The added weight can help reduce anxiety and promote feelings of relaxation, which can help you fall asleep faster, according to Logan Foley, a certified sleep-science coach and editorial director at Sleep Foundation. Plus weighted blankets are just really comforting. Think of the pressure that an X-ray vest at the dentist’s office provides, but cozier — and without the harrowing dental procedure that usually comes with it. Or, as David Rubin, a certified sleep-science coach and director of product testing at the Sleep Doctor, explains, using a weighted blanket feels like “being swaddled or held in a firm hug,” which he says can increase serotonin, which in turn influences how long and how well you sleep.

When I tried my first weighted blanket a few years ago, I was skeptical of its calming properties as I’ve thankfully always been a good sleeper. Weighted blankets still are not a regular part of my sleeping ritual, but now that I’ve tested a few over the years, their heaviness noticeably calms and soothes me and helps me get to sleep more quickly. Recently, brands have been offering smaller sizes like throws as well as lower weights, which strike the balance of added weight without the bulk and could be a good place to start for those interested in trying one out. To help you find the best for your individual needs, I tested a few options and consulted a dozen experts about their favorites to bring you the best weighted blankets in a range of sizes for every budget and sleep preference, whether they’re filled with beads, made from chunky yarn, or simply use heavier fabrics.

Updated on November 3, 2026
I added two new weighted blankets, the Cocoon and the Lola. All other products have been checked for price and availability.

Weighted blankets come in a variety of different materials and knits, which I’ll get to below, but the most important factor when shopping for a weighted blanket is the weight, says Foley. Dr. Raj Dasgupta, sleep specialist and clinical associate professor of medicine at the University of Southern California’s Keck School of Medicine, advises buyers to choose a weighted blanket that comes in at about 8 to 12 percent of the user’s body weight. Sleep specialist Dr. Brandon Peters gives this example: “For an adult who weighs 200 pounds, a 20-pound blanket would be appropriate.” Any heavier and the blanket will be more uncomfortable than soothing. In our experience, most blankets weigh between 10 and 25 pounds, but occasionally you’ll see a mere five-pounder or a hefty one up to 35 pounds. As Keith Cushner, the executive director of product testing at Sleep Foundation, put it, “As long as you get the weight right, you’ll enjoy a weighted blanket.” Relatedly, all the blankets come in a range of sizes, from ones meant for use by one person or those that can be used across a bed for two.

As with comforters, the material comes down to personal preference. Over the years, manufacturers have come out with more options for colors and styles, Cushner says, from knitted blankets to ones that look like standard comforters with duvet covers to faux-fur styles, so you can choose what works best for you.

Sweaty sleepers may think they’ll forever be excluded from the weighted blanket club because a heavy layer can feel very warm. However, there are a few out there that can actually feel cooler during sleep. Made from materials like Tencel and bamboo, these versions tend to be more lightweight and temperature-regulating than their polyester or flannel counterparts. (For more specifics, I rounded up a bunch of cooling options here.)

Weighted blankets are most commonly filled with plastic, glass, or steel beads; grains; beans; or even sand. Occasionally, they have no filling and get their weight from the hefty fabric. As I wrote in the companion story on the best cooling weighted blankets, glass beads, besides being more environmentally friendly than plastic, are a bit more cooling than other fillings. Whatever the filling, to make sure it won’t shift over time, it needs to be sewn into quilted squares or somehow made to stay in place. Even distribution is key to a functional weighted blanket; it won’t work quite as well if all the filling falls to one end.

As far as how durable they are, Cushner says that weighted blankets “hold up as long as they look good,” like any regular, non-weighted blankets. Most of them come with removable covers that can be machine-washed, and even knit blankets can, per some manufacturers, go in the laundry.

Weight: 10, 15, 20, and 25 pounds | Material: Available in Tencel lyocell, cotton, and velvet jumbo yarn | Filling: Chunky knit | Maintenance: Machine washable

Longtime Strategist readers shouldn’t be surprised to find the Bearaby weighted blanket at the top of our list. (It’s also our top choice for the best overall cooling weighted blanket, a favorite of Strategist staffers, and is even celebrity-approved.) What makes it unique is that, unlike other weighted blankets, the Bearaby doesn’t have a filling. Instead, it’s hand knit with a thick, chunky yarn made with layers of fabric, which creates the heft. And thanks to the open-knit construction, it’s inherently breathable, a boon to hot sleepers. It’s arguably the best-looking weighted blanket out there, too, resembling something cozy as opposed to therapeutic.

I tested a 15-pounder and found it to be extremely comforting and calming. I put it over my comforter during colder months and felt cozy and “pressed down” in a way that instantly put me to sleep. It’s admittedly harder to move around underneath it, because it’s so heavy, but that contributed to a deeper sleep. I will note that because of its construction, it’s a bit cumbersome to store and carry, and the loops require adjusting from time to time, so you’ll want to keep that in mind. Senior editor Jen Trolio, who has owned the velvet version for over three years and has given others as gifts, was first drawn to its look and is now “all in” on the Bearaby, though she notes that the “chunkiness can be an issue” for some, especially if you’re sharing a bed with someone. Strategist junior writer Bella Druckman sleeps with one every night: “It actually relaxes my body as I fall asleep,” she says. “I know experts always say that, but I didn’t realize how true it was until I tried it myself. It helps me calm down when I’m restless before bed.” The Bearaby is available in 10-, 15-, 20-, and 25-pound weights and comes in three materials (cotton, Tencel, and velvet), though it should be noted that not all materials encompass the full range of sizes. Bearaby also offers the nicest and broadest color options, including lavender, butternut, and jade, depending on the style. As far as maintenance goes, it’s machine washable, but Trolio notes that it takes a while to dry.

Weight: 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 25, 30, 40, and 50 pounds | Material: Cotton, nylon, or microfiber | Filling: Glass beads | Maintenance: Machine washable

If you’re looking to dip your toe into the world of weighted blankets, consider ones from YnM, which, unlike Bearaby, are filled with glass beads (and are the more traditional style of weighted blanket), more affordable, and might be a little easier to wrangle than a chunky knit. An Amazon bestseller, it comes in the largest range of weights on this list, from 5 to 30 pounds, and in different materials including cotton, nylon, and microfiber. It’s a favorite of former Strategist associate editor Jenna Milliner-Waddell, who has owned the cotton weighted blanket since 2019. She defines her life “pre–YnM blanket and post–YnM blanket.” “Pre-YnM, it took me what felt like forever to fall asleep. My post-YnM sleep life, though, is very different,” she writes. “Using the blanket, I couldn’t tell you how long it takes me to fall asleep, because I’m actually sleeping instead of having nightly staring contests with my ceiling.” It’s made of seven layers and is filled with glass beads that are distributed between 2” x 2” pockets.

YnM labels the blanket as cooling because of its many layers of breathable fabric and glass beads. But Milliner-Waddell clarifies, saying, “lying under it doesn’t feel like an ice bath, but as someone who sleeps hot, I will say using the blanket doesn’t make me any hotter, even on warmer nights.” As far as durability goes, after owning it for three years, Milliner-Waddell says that it’s “held up great, with no tears or staining, and all the beads are still in the right spot.” It comes in a bunch of fun colors, like sky blue and avocado, and cute patterns, depending on the size and material. While the instructions say that the entire blanket is machine washable (it does not come with a cover), reviews on Amazon are mixed on whether that’s a good idea. Your best bet would be to get a separate removable duvet cover so you have to wash the actual blanket less.

Weight: 5.8 pounds | Material: Cotton | Filling: Cotton | Maintenance: Machine washable

Many weighted blankets can be too cumbersome to use every day, so I was interested in testing a few options that had extra heft to them without being a full-on weighted blanket. Coyuchi’s newly launched Dreamweight throw is a lower-weight weighted blanket that I can see myself using on a daily basis. It’s made of organic cotton inside and out and constructed with a gauzy matelassé weave that makes it look and feel like a lived-in quilt. Despite its 5.8-pound weight, the fabric gives it a breathable quality and is also quite soft to the touch. It’s a well-made, heirloom-quality blanket that also looks really elegant.

Weight: 5.4 pounds (medium), 10.14 pounds (large) | Material: Polyester | Filling: Polyester | Maintenance: Machine washable

Cocoon, maker of plush faux-fur blankets, just released a weighted version, and I got the chance to test one for this story. The first thing I noticed: It’s made of polyester and is one of the softest blankets I have ever felt in this cozy category. I got the medium size, which measures a standard throw size of 50 by 60 inches and weighs slightly less than the Coyuchi above, coming in at 5.4 pounds. The product description says the weighted version is denser than the brand’s classic blanket and has an 800 GSM (grams per square meter, or the measure of a fabric’s weight) per layer compared with between 500 and 600 for the original. The heft comes from the fabric, and to be frank, I didn’t find it felt too different in weight from my beloved Pottery Barn faux-fur throw. (I even weighed it on the scale, and it’s the same weight, 5.4 pounds.) But it’s less bulky than the Pottery Barn blanket and easier to use because it’s thinner. I can pull it over my lap while reading or watching TV. I can throw it over my bed for a quick nap, and I don’t have to worry about the layers separating. It’s honestly a gorgeous blanket if you’re looking for a fuzzy and weighted — but not too heavy — throw.

Weight: 12.5 pounds | Material: Polyester | Filling: None | Maintenance: Machine washable

Here’s another option that looks like a traditional throw but has qualities of a weighted blanket. Cozy Earth makes a plush faux-fur blanket available in an “extra-weight” option in addition to its regular throws. It weighs 12.5 pounds (the regular throws range from 6.2 to 11 pounds in weight), is furry on both sides, and is very thick, which is where the weight comes from (not glass beads). Compared with the Cocoon, it’s much thicker — like a flat giant teddy bear — and therefore a little more cumbersome to use. I would say this is a bed blanket, whereas the Cocoon is more portable. Still, it is very soft, comforting, and plush. I could imagine using it on the floor like a fuzzy mat, too.

Weight: 12, 15, 20, and 25 pounds | Material: Cotton | Filling: Glass beads | Maintenance: Machine washable

For those looking for a glass-filled weighted blanket covered in cotton, Baloo makes a very nice one that comes in throw, full/queen, and king sizes, the latter two which allow you to share one with a partner. Trolio uses the Bearaby on herself, but when she wants to cover the entire bed with a weighted blanket so her husband is under it as well, she opts for the queen-size Baloo. “For actual beds and especially in partner scenarios, the glass beads are nice for a sleeker, slimmer look,” she says, adding that knits are better as a throw. Because she prefers to “sleep under the equivalent of a pile of bricks,” Trolio pairs the queen with a 12-pound throw on her side for extra weight. Even with the double layer, the bed still looks neat, and she’s not burning up under them, either. The cotton itself feels “very smooth, possibly even sateen-y,” says Trolio.

When former Strategist senior writer Karen Iorio Adelson tested the blanket, she reported that it was comfortable for a hot sleeper like herself. “I felt cooler sleeping under the Baloo than most of the other blankets,” she says. While not specifically labeled “cooling,” the cotton material actually plays a huge part in the breathability of the Baloo. “We sleep more deeply in a cool environment. Heat loss and temperature regulation often occur from our feet at night. This is why people may kick their feet out from under the covers at night,” explains Peters, adding, “A material like cotton is more breathable, allowing for natural cooling.” The blanket has a thin profile, further contributing to its comfort, and the glass beads help with airflow because they’re not as tightly packed. It’s also machine washable, but Trolio prefers using a duvet cover for protection as it (and many glass-filled weighted blankets) comes with corner ties for that very purpose. She adds, though, that its weight makes it hard to keep the blanket from moving around inside the cover.

Weight: 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 22, 25, 27, 30, and 32 pounds | Material: Bamboo viscose | Filling: Glass beads | Maintenance: Machine washable

Here’s a weighted blanket that’s made of bamboo viscose that Ben Trapskin, founder of Sleep Sherpa recommends. “It is one of the smoothest-feeling weighted blankets I have used,” he says, thanks to the bamboo fabric cover that, according to him, “has a silky feel and helps keep you cool.” The glass-bead-filled blanket incorporates layers of microfiber, which Trapskin says “gives it a more consistent feel, more like a regular blanket.” The extra padding “makes it so that you don’t hear the glass beads shifting when you move,” he adds. Another feature he calls out is the fact that it comes with a travel case. Because of it, “It’s easier to fold and put away than other weighted blankets I have used.” It’s machine washable, but you can buy a separate cover for added protection.

Weight: 3.5 pounds (small), 7.5 pounds (medium), 10.5 pounds (large), 17.5 (extra-large) | Material: Polyester | Filling: Glass beads | Maintenance: Machine washable

The weighted blanket from Lola is closer to a traditional version because the heft comes from its filling of glass beads (in addition to the fabric’s inherent density). Druckman, who uses her Bearaby weighted blanket every night, has been testing the Lola weighted blanket for a few weeks. She already owns and loves the original Lola blanket, calling it “soft like how I imagine a chinchilla would feel.” The original blanket is heavier than your average throw, she says, but the addition of glass beads “makes it heavy enough that it becomes a true weighted blanket.” (The product description doesn’t list how much the blanket weighs, but she says the large size feels comparable to her ten-pound Bearaby.) She’s had it only for a month but says “I find that I sleep more soundly underneath it.” Druckman calls the Lola ideal for winter and prefers her Bearaby blanket in the summer because it doesn’t trap heat like the Lola.

Weight: 8, 12, 15, 20, and 25 pounds | Material: Cotton | Filling: None | Maintenance: Machine washable

Silk & Snow makes a knitted weighted blanket ranging from 8 to 25 pounds in weight. I requested the lowest weight because I wanted to use it more like a throw. The brand bills the 8-pounder as a kids’ blanket. It has a looser weave than Bearaby’s knitted blanket, which explains its more manageable size. I found it interesting that the “yarns” were formed by flat pieces of cotton that have been twisted and folded. (Bearaby’s yarns are tubes that are filled with cotton batting.) Because the spaces are bigger between the yarns, you have to be more careful when handling it so that it doesn’t stretch out too much, but the weight makes it manageable. It has a bit more of a rustic look thanks to the folded yarns and looks less like a weighted blanket, if that is a consideration in choosing one.

Weight: 1.5 kg (3.3 pounds), 2 kg (4.4 pounds), and 3 kg (6.6 pounds) | Material: Cotton | Filling: None | Maintenance: Machine washable

Blankets from Australia-based Woven Woven are also knitted but resemble a traditional (non-chunky) cotton blanket thanks to a proprietary knitting technique that evenly distributes the weight throughout the blanket. Though they are made for children and range in size from 1.5 kg (3.3 pounds) to 3 kg (6.6 pounds), Strategist deputy editor Simone Kitchens has been sharing it with her daughter. Kitchens love its smaller dimensions, as the blanket doesn’t take over the whole bed and instead covers only her upper body. “It’s not on my legs, which always makes me feel a little trapped,” she says. “It adds this perfect amount of weight to my upper half and is a perfect mix of weight and a little warmth, especially for now when it’s freezing outside.” She points out that it’s very nicely woven and goes with her bedding more seamlessly than other weighted blanket styles she has tried. Kitchens got the 1.5 kg with her daughter in mind originally but found that she would kick it off at night. Kitchens would have maybe gone with a heavier one for herself, but she still loves using it on top of her comforter without feeling trapped by it.

entry.title: All My Makeup Is Sticks Now
entry.summary: Just about every brand is making a stick blush, concealer, contour, or eye shadow, and they’re supremely easy to use and travel with.
entry.content:
As a beauty writer, I’m constantly trying out new makeup launches. My desk and vanity are strewn with blushes, foundations, concealers, and bronzers, a microcosm of what’s trending in the beauty world. And what I’ve noticed over the last year or so is that, slowly but surely, my makeup routine has been overtaken by sticks.

Stick cosmetics are not exactly groundbreaking. But there’s something to be said for the fact that every beauty brand, whether it’s launching a concealer or an eye shadow, seems to be offering it up as a stick in lieu of liquid or powder formulas. Stick makeup’s biggest draw is that it’s supremely easy to use; most stick formulas have a cream consistency that melts into skin without leaving any patchiness. You can apply them directly to your face and blend using just your fingers, but they also play perfectly well with brushes, which I prefer (less mess!). That method squares nicely with the current minimal, easygoing approach to makeup and feels less intimidating to newbies. Plus you can throw a stick into a bag without worrying about whether it’ll spill or shatter — which, having once ruined the interior of a Boat and Tote with a broken foundation bottle, is something I can very much appreciate. Here are all the makeup sticks I’m currently using on repeat.

I was a little nervous to try Lancôme’s stick version of its Teint Idole foundation — I’ve tested the brand’s long-wearing liquid format before and found it too heavy-duty for everyday wear. I prefer a finish that’s more skinlike and breathable, and remarkably, the stick version of the foundation nailed it. I swipe it directly on my face, then blend it out with a foundation brush; it feels like I’m wearing nothing but still delivers a light veil of coverage while letting the natural texture of my skin peek through. The only downside is that the packaging is a little fragile — I dropped one on the ground, and the stick broke. But it’s still usable; I just have to be mindful when twisting the applicator up and down.

For any spots that need some extra coverage, I use this dual-ended concealer stick from DIBS Beauty. One side is a concealer, and the other is a brightener; the two can be combined to customize the coverage and help hide dark circles or tired under eyes, but I don’t tend to get dark shadows under my eyes, so I mostly use the concealer side. The cream format tends to highlight flakiness more than liquid concealer, so I wouldn’t use it on something like a healing zit. But for freckles and dark marks, it blends easily and covers them right up.

I first heard about Canadian beauty brand 19/99 through Amanda Dobbins, who’s a big fan of the brand’s highlight stick. Intrigued by her rave review, I asked the brand to send me its full range of beauty sticks for testing, and though the highlight and blush are both lovely, I’ve been using the contour stick the most. The lighter color, Tea, is just the right shade to give me a bronze-y glow without looking too stark. I draw a line below my cheekbones and around my jawline, plus a few dots around my hairline, then blend it out with an angled brush, though I’ve also used my fingers in a pinch. It seems somewhat sturdier than Lancome’s Shape Stick, too; it’s bounced around in my carry-on and emerged none the worse for wear.

This Patrick Ta stick is smaller and slimmer than the 19/99 stick, which makes it more precise for contouring smaller areas around my brows, nose bridge, and lips. I have two shades, Shape and Silhouette, and will rotate between them depending on how defined I want my contour to be. I’ve also used them as eye shadows in a pinch — they’re very creamy and easy to blend, so I can apply a bit on my finger to warm it up and then dab it onto the corners of my eyes to give them a bit more dimension. The sticks are also conveniently dual-ended — the other side is a brush you can use for blending. I personally find the attached brush to be a tad dense, so when I’m at home I use a fluffier brush, but I’ll forgo it when I’m traveling to save space in my makeup bag.

Milk recently overhauled its entire hero line, the Milk Sticks collection, just in time for the brand’s tenth anniversary. There’s a Lip + Cheek blush stick with both matte and satin finishes, a bronzer stick, a contour stick, a highlight stick, and a lip liner. The blush stick is my favorite. I’ve been using the shade Enigma, a rosy beige, and it’s one of the best multi-sticks I’ve ever tried. The formula is infused with skin-friendly ingredients like hyaluronic acid, ceramides, and jojoba oil, so it feels nice and hydrating on any flaky areas around my cheeks or lips. The product itself glides on smoothly, blends into a softly diffuse blur, and doesn’t feel waxy or tacky. When I apply it across my nose bridge, I look like I’ve just spent a day out in the sun, even if all I did was peck away at my laptop. If I’m doing my makeup in a rush, I’ll pop some on my eyes too for an easy monochromatic look.

Another blush stick I’ve been using a lot lately is this Haus Labs one. I have the shade Cinnamon, a peachy beige. While the Milk Makeup stick above has a natural satin finish, this one is more dewy, with a glassy gleam to it — texturally, it feels a little more “wet” than the Milk blush stick. It’s also quite pigmented, so a little goes a long way. In fact, I’ll often combine the two, just to give my blush look more dimension; I go in first with the Milk to create a nice dusky, peachy base, then add in the Haus Labs toward the center of my face and nose bridge to deepen the flush.

This Goop Beauty Highlight Stick is everything I wanted Glossier’s Haloscope to be. While I really had to squint to see whether anything even happened after applying Haloscope, I can immediately spot a radiant shimmer after applying Goop Beauty’s. I have the shade Aura, a pearlescent Champagne that has the chameleonic ability to enhance any blush color I pair it with. I dot it along my cheekbones, Cupid’s bow, and brow bone, and sometimes along my eyelids and inner-eye corner.

entry.title: I Can’t Stop Wearing Polo Sweaters
entry.summary: I found favorites from With Nothing Underneath, Madewell, and Banana Republic.
entry.content:
Every autumn, there’s no shortage of simple crewneck sweaters, but I couldn’t help but notice another style at the front of practically every knitwear section this fall. With its more structured collar and vintage-inspired prep, the polo sweater is one I’ve been missing from my closet until recently. There are plenty online — from Madewell and With Nothing Underneath to Quince and Banana Republic — so I set out to test polo sweaters for women, leaning into natural fibers (like merino wool, organic cotton, and cashmere) since I’ve been consciously shifting away from wearing synthetics in my closet to reduce the plastic in my life. Below are my favorites, from classics you’ll wear through every season to other picks for layering with your go-to white button-down this winter. (For reference, I’m five-foot-five and usually wear a size small in tops. I also have a shorter torso, broader shoulders, and a 34-inch band size.).

I’ve been super impressed with all of the knitwear I’ve tried from London-based brand With Nothing Underneath (also known as WNU). Many of the pieces are inspired by British heritage and men’s tailoring, so I knew I needed to test its newest polo sweater. The Renfrew Jumper is made of yak wool, which is known for being warm and soft like cashmere but keeps its shape better and is more hard-wearing for every day. Yak is also naturally odor-resistant, which makes it easy to care for. I love that this knit is more textured and thicker than many of the cashmere sweaters in my closet, and the fit is perfectly oversize and boxy through the midsection. The ribbed hemline means there can be a casual rolled silhouette around my waist or I can have it pulled down around my hips. The striped pattern definitely pulls from traditional rugby and polo shirts, but there’s a dash of English country charm thanks to the colors.

Madewell’s SoftWool yarn, which is made of 100 percent merino wool, is used in many of its popular pieces, from V-necks to cardigans to beanies. I was completely new to SoftWool until I tried this stripe-y mid-weight polo sweater. As someone who’s sensitive to itchy fabrics, I was very impressed by how soft this felt on my skin, and I never overheated while wearing it. The sweater has a relaxed cut that isn’t too fitted or too boxy, plus it has a ribbed hemline and cuffs. I opted for my usual size small but could have easily sized up to a medium for a looser fit on my five-foot-five frame. The fit was more than ideal on my shorter torso, but sizing up might help any long-in-the-body folks.

I’ve always found Quince’s cashmere to be on the lighter and more delicate side, but this polo sweater actually felt a tad thicker and more plush. The collar combined with the longer placket felt more masculine when done up completely, but I prefer it layered over a tee or tank and unbuttoned to create a nice V-neck. If you plan on wearing it over a button-down like in some of Quince’s product images, I recommend sizing up to ensure there’s enough room in the shoulders.

I own this polo sweater in two colorways because the cotton version works as a multi-season wardrobe staple. It was a comfortable summer layering piece on cooler nights, and I’ve continued to wear it on balmy fall days. The mid-weight cotton reminds me of the knit used in the J.Crew Rollneck and the Tiny Rollneck in my closet, but it’s not as tight, so it does feel less durable. It is also cropped, but I find it extremely easy to style with high-rise bottoms, including jeans and pleated trousers.

Similar to the Quince number above, this J.Crew sweater doesn’t have any buttons, so the design relies on the polo collar (or Johnny collar, to be more precise). The subtle V-neckline gives it a clean yet casual look. The cotton fabric is more lightweight than that of the Quince polo sweater above, but it has remained soft and pill-free even after multiple wears and washes. It has a relaxed shape, but I would say it runs slightly oversize. I wish I’d gone with my usual small; I made the mistake of picking a size medium, which I decided to keep, but the hem ends past my hip bones — I would prefer it to be a tad shorter. There are slits on either side of the hem for some extra breathing room and to prevent any bunching up at the waist.

This polo sweater is technically a cardigan, but I couldn’t resist since it’s made of only merino wool. It’s one of the thinnest knits on this list, which made it great for layering under a jacket or blazer. The fit wasn’t too tight, but since it is clingier, I decided to go up to a medium so there was no pulling along the placket (I’m in the C-cup range). The long sleeves are another bonus if you have broad shoulders like me or longer arms. My favorite detail is the snap buttons on the shoulder that provide some visible structure and give the sweater a modern, slightly utilitarian look without being overly flashy.

I’ve reported on other impressive Lands’ End basics — like its well-made riding boots and classic fisherman cardigans — so I knew it was important to try a polo sweater from its cashmere line. The cashmere is Grade A, which means it was made from the thinnest and longest goat-hair fibers, translating to a softer feel. Writer Erika Veurink previously wrote about the men’s polo sweater and said it makes her feel dressed up for work with “zero effort.” And I couldn’t agree more after trying the women’s version. The ribbed hem holds its shape well, and it can be worn buttoned up or with the collar open over a T-shirt. There are plenty of color options available, plus it comes in regular and plus sizes. Bonus: Lands’ End gives you the option to personalize it with your initials or a word for an extra $11.

entry.title: Steve Kornacki’s Election Night Khakis Are on Sale
entry.summary: Here’s hoping for a different outcome than the last time he wore them.
entry.content:
It’s Election Night once more, and maybe you’d prefer to forget how our democracy hangs in the balance. Here’s a lighter serving of political coverage instead. During the 2020 election, MSNBC’s infamous numbers guy Steve Kornacki reported hour after hour while wearing the same pair of pants. We did some sleuthing to determine that they were Gap’s Modern Khakis in Straight Fit. And then he wore them again in 2024, and while you’re probably not hoping for a repeat of that ill-fated night, there’s one kinda-sorta good omen today: The same pants are on sale.

While the original shade — palomino brown — is no longer available in this style, a bunch of other colorways are 40 percent off (with an additional 10 percent off if you use Gap’s app). That brings them down to just $35 from an original price of $60. Palomino brown is available in the Heavyweight Twill Baggy Khakis, which are similar, just a bit thicker and wider.

We don’t yet know what pants Kornacki will wear today while he’s on the Big Board as Chief Data Analyst at NBC News, but if I was in his place, I’d definitely be stocking up on the Gap Khakis. If he has any time to spare today, that is.
